boundary: This ledger records LINKAGE, not coverage. A status says which shipped mechanical controls cite a rule, and each control carries a residue naming what it does not catch; the residue is the honest half of every claim. None of the statuses means a rule is enforced: gate-linked means at least one deterministic repository gate cites the rule, hook-linked means at least one runtime hook cites it and no gate does, prose-only means no shipped control cites it and the rule binds through the governing prose alone. Each gate and hook row carries its class letter; a rule linked only through class c gates is linked only for a recognizable subset of its surface. A preview hook is not a shipped control: it is published in .preview/ for manual installation, outside the plugin. The previews list names the declared preview hooks whose own description names the rule, and a declaration never changes a status; a hook row carrying channel preview is a preview-channel hook, which links its rule as any hook row does. Nothing in this file is a completeness or coverage measure, and deriving a score from it misreads it.

hooks.residue: Covers the required-absolute file_path of Read, Write, and Edit and the required-absolute notebook_path of NotebookEdit (absolute by each tool's own contract, so the relative-to-a-named-root carve-out never applies to them), plus the OPTIONAL path search root of Glob and Grep (which should be absolute), and the MultiEdit file_path kept for LEGACY COMPATIBILITY. Each field name is bound to a Claude Code tool schema (Read/Write/Edit -> file_path, NotebookEdit -> notebook_path, Glob/Grep -> optional path); MultiEdit -> file_path is retained as a legacy-compatibility wire (MultiEdit is NOT in the current Claude Code built-in tool index, so its mapping is kept only so an adopter on an older or re-enabled MultiEdit is still covered, never an assertion that MultiEdit is a current tool). This STRUCTURED coverage binds ONLY those enumerated tool schemas: a path carried in any OTHER tool field, tool, or parameter, or in Bash command text, is out of scope here (the sibling abs-paths-bash floor covers only a cd/pushd destination and a redirect target in Bash, nothing else). Absoluteness is judged by the runtime's own path semantics (PurePosixPath/PureWindowsPath.is_absolute), so a drive-RELATIVE 'C:file', a bare 'C:', and a rooted-but-driveless leading-backslash path are correctly NOT absolute, while a POSIX '/x', a drive-absolute 'C:\x'/'C:/x', and a UNC '\\server\share' are; a '~'-prefixed path is not expanded and is not absolute. Honours the carve-out: the relative search PATTERN of Glob and Grep is legitimately relative to its named root and is never judged, and a rootless call (no path) names the current directory as that root and is allowed. Fails CLOSED: a tool_input that is not a readable mapping, or a required file_path/notebook_path that is absent or not a non-empty string, denies rather than passing (closing the earlier fail-open where a malformed tool_input collapsed to an empty mapping and took the search-root allow branch). Does NOT judge whether an absolute path points at the INTENDED target (absoluteness is not intent), and is platform=claude-code only. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took under 0.01 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

A SEPARATE best-effort Bash layer of abspth, distinct from the structured typed-path guard (abs-paths), whose structured coverage binds only the enumerated tool schemas and never Bash command text. This is a CONSERVATIVE FLOOR that NEVER asks and, with ONE exception, NEVER denies: it ALLOWS-WITH-AN-INFORMATIONAL-NOTE (NO-ASK posture; the user's own permission flow still governs, and every ASK/ASKS below is the retired term for that allow-with-note outcome, since absolute paths are a convention, not a hazard). The ONE DENY exception (a review finding): a DESTRUCTIVE TRUNCATING redirect (a '>'/'>|'/'&>' or a '>&'-to-a-file) whose TARGET is RELATIVE or OPAQUE DENIES-and-educates, because truncation ZEROES its target and a cwd-dependent relative or unverified target could destroy the WRONG file; an append '>>', a read '<'/'<>', and every cd/pushd DESTINATION position never deny (they note). It judges ONLY two positions that silently resolve against the current working directory, a cd/pushd DESTINATION operand and a redirection TARGET, and NEVER an arbitrary command operand (a relative path argument to any other command is deliberately NOT judged, to avoid over-firing). A relative or unresolvable such position is NOTED; an absolute one, an UNQUOTED CURRENT-USER tilde destination ('~' or '~/x', which the shell expands to $HOME so it is cwd-independent), a bare 'cd'/'pushd' and the OLDPWD 'cd -' (both only absent ANY leading inline env-assignment, see below), the real cd/pushd option flags (cd -L/-P/-e/-@, pushd -n, singly or bundled), a pushd stack rotation (+N/-N), and a numeric/'-' descriptor duplication (2>&1) allow. The tilde-ALLOW is NARROWED to the current-user forms and gated on a WHOLE-TILDE-PREFIX-UNQUOTED signal, NOT on the broader token-wide opacity flag: it is True only when the token begins with an unquoted '~' AND the ENTIRE tilde-prefix (from that '~' up to the first UNQUOTED '/', or end of word) is unquoted and unescaped, which is exactly when bash performs tilde-expansion. So a QUOTED leading tilde, EVEN with an unquoted expansion/glob/brace TAIL (the "~"/x*, '~'/x?, "~"/$V, "~/repo"* forms), is NOT tilde-expanded (the '~' is quoted, the word stays RELATIVE) and ASKS, as does a fully-quoted '~'/'~/x', an escaped '\~/...', and an empty-quote-preceded '""~/x' (bash expands only a '~' at the very start of the word). It ALSO ASKS a leading unquoted '~' whose PREFIX itself carries a quote or escape BEFORE the first unquoted '/' - '~"/x"', '~'' (empty single-quote), '~""/x', '~'/x'', '~"/"$V', and a '~' followed by an escaped '/' - because any quote or escape in the tilde-prefix disables bash expansion and the word stays RELATIVE, EVEN when the DECODED token is fully literal '~/x' with no opacity. Only a quote or expansion AFTER the prefix-closing unquoted '/' does not block expansion, so the genuine 'cd ~/$VAR' (prefix is the bare '~', the '$VAR' sits after the '/') STAYS ALLOW. A later hardening pass propagates this SAME clean-leading-tilde signal into the redirect-TARGET classification (previously the redirect parser discarded it, so a '> ~/x' target was classed opaque and ASKED, inconsistent with 'cd ~/x'): a redirect target whose whole leading tilde-prefix is clean/unquoted now ALLOWS ('> ~/x', '> ~/"x"', '> ~/$V', and the bare '> ~'), while a quoted or complex-prefix tilde target ('> "~"/x', '> ~"/x"') keeps its opacity and ASKS - exactly matching the cd tilde rule. A '~user'/'~user/x' names another account's home whose EXISTENCE the hook cannot verify (an unresolved login name leaves the word RELATIVE), so it is NOT proven absolute and ASKS (the conservative call; a '~user' cd is rare); the '~-'/'~+'/'~N' directory-stack forms likewise ASK. Only the closed option forms are treated as non-destinations, and '--' ENDS option processing, so a genuine relative directory name that begins '-'/'+' is still the destination and ASKS ('cd -- -rel', 'cd +rel', 'cd -rel'), while a lone '-' AFTER '--' is still the $OLDPWD shortcut in bash and ALLOWS ('cd -- -') and a post-'--' directory literally named '--' stays relative and ASKS ('cd -- --'); an opaque '$VAR' destination cannot be proven absolute and ASKS. ANY leading inline env-assignment PREFIXING a cd/pushd (any variable name, '=' or the append '+=' form) can redirect where the cwd-INDEPENDENT destinations land: an inline OLDPWD=/OLDPWD+= redirects the lone '-' ($OLDPWD) shortcut and an inline HOME=/HOME+= redirects the bare 'cd' ($HOME default), in each case to a value the floor cannot prove absolute (e.g. '..'). CONSERVATIVE CONSOLIDATION: rather than enumerate OLDPWD/HOME by name (which missed the '+=' append form and the bare-cd HOME default entirely - the earlier under-blocks), the floor takes the stance that the mere PRESENCE of ANY leading assignment makes those two otherwise-cwd-independent destinations ASK, so 'OLDPWD=.. cd -- -', 'OLDPWD+=.. cd -', 'HOME=.. cd', 'HOME+=.. cd', and 'HOME=.. pushd' all ASK, while a plain zero-assignment 'cd -'/'cd -- -'/bare 'cd' keeps its ALLOW. This is DELIBERATELY conservative in two disclosed ways: (a) a BENIGN leading assignment on a cwd-independent form ('FOO=x cd -', 'FOO=x cd') also ASKS, the accepted cost of not name-enumerating; and (b) an assignment token whose NAME was quoted or escaped ('"OLDPWD"=.. cd -', 'OLD"PWD"=.. cd -', 'OLDP\WD=.. cd -') is a COMMAND to bash (command-not-found; cd never runs), but its DECODED form is assignment-shaped ('OLDPWD=..'), so the floor reads it as a leading assignment and ASKS - an intentional over-fire on an assignment-shaped token bash would reject anyway, NOT chased with assignment-name quote provenance. It reuses the shared quote/redirect-aware lexer (_lex_command), so a redirect anywhere is seen and a quoted metacharacter is not miscounted; but the lexer is NOT a shell interpreter: it cannot resolve an ALIAS, a shell FUNCTION, eval, a command substitution, or a VARIABLE EXPANSION, so a cd or redirect reached through any of those, or whose command word is not literally cd/pushd (a wrapper, a PATH-shadowed name, an absolute /usr/bin/cd is resolved by basename but an aliased 'cd' is not), is not judged. An operand carrying an unexpanded expansion never reads as absolute unless it is literally rooted, so 'cd $DIR' ASKS while 'cd /$X' allows; a redirect target formed from an expansion is classified opaque and ASKS. A bare filename passed to an unknown command is indistinguishable from data and is not judged. Absoluteness is NOT intent: an absolute cd or redirect can still point at the wrong directory. An unparseable construct (a heredoc, here-string, process substitution, '{fd}>' redirect, or an unbalanced quote or escape) is handled by PARTIAL lex: the COMPLETE segments before it AND the positions of the still-open IN-PROGRESS segment that were fully parsed BEFORE it are still inspected, so an earlier resolvable relative cd/redirect - whether in an earlier segment ('cd rel; cat <<EOF...') OR the redirect target of the same in-progress segment parsed before the construct ('cat > out.txt <<EOF...' and 'cat > out.txt <(...)' ASK on out.txt) - still ASKS rather than being discarded; ONLY a cd/redirect position WITHIN or AFTER the unparseable construct is left uninspected and ALLOWED, a disclosed residual rather than an over-ask on every such command. A missing tool_name denies (the shared fail-closed contract); a missing or unreadable command string ASKS rather than silently allowing. It is best-effort against the accidental case, not an adversary, and is platform=claude-code only. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 1.37 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

Within the Bash hook's recognized or apparent direct-commit surface, commits deny unless an admitted command shape proves their target worktree and non-protected local branch, or the narrow lone no-remote policy exemption applies. Unknown wrappers, unsupported preceding effects or control flow, accompanying repository/configuration mechanisms, non-cosmetic ambient GIT_* overrides, and failed probes deny. A plain absolute git -C /absolute/repo commit is supported only when its applicable branch is proved non-protected and no accompanying mechanism or unknown preceding effect invalidates that proof. Protected names are exactly main and master, case-sensitive. Unknown and proved-protected states are distinct internally; both deny without an applicable certificate. There is no unproved-commit allow-note and no ASK outcome.

Certificates: A is a plain session commit with an intact absolute cwd binding and validated non-protected local HEAD. B is a commit with exactly one separated, nonempty, absolute literal -C operand, a proved worktree identity, and applicable non-protected branch state. C is a commit gated through an uninterrupted && chain by an admitted switch addressing the same proved worktree. D is a policy exemption, not evidence of a non-protected destination: exactly one plain session commit on a valid protected local HEAD, with remote absence proved by successful configuration and legacy-common-directory checks. Unknown remote state withholds D. Compounds, -C, redirects, wrappers, assignments, and opaque arguments cannot obtain D. A valid unborn symbolic local HEAD can establish a branch name; detached, malformed, missing, or unreadable HEAD cannot.

Every committing shape requires complete admitted syntax and literal arguments, including quoted literal message data. The only Git prefixes are git commit and git -C /absolute/repo commit; arguments after the commit verb remain commit arguments, judged by other guards for their own policies. Compounds admit only &&-connected segments: argument-free :, true, or false; exactly printf %s LITERAL; exactly cd ABSOLUTE_LITERAL_DIRECTORY; git switch EXISTING_LOCAL_BRANCH; git switch -c NEW_LOCAL_BRANCH; git checkout -b NEW_LOCAL_BRANCH; and separately certified commits. Switch forms may use the same exact absolute -C prefix. A preceding admitted cd invalidates session binding; an explicit target can establish B afterward. An admitted trailing cd cannot change an earlier commit destination. Unknown segments before or after a commit deny the whole commit-bearing command. Exactly lone literal git commit --help and git commit -h are non-committing help forms; message values, pathspecs, and global-option values spelling --help do not supply that exemption.

INTENTIONAL OVER-DENY: harmless global options, leading assignments (including the removed discard-override prefix), wrappers even with harmless options, attached/relative/repeated/empty -C, redirects, unsupported switch syntax, complex compounds and non-&& separators, and detached commits are rejected even when a particular execution would be harmless. Absolute -C does not repair protected branch state, unknown prior mutations, ambient overrides, or failed probes. After arbitrary work such as make test, issue the commit as a SEPARATE hook invocation that obtains fresh state; make test && git -C /absolute/repo commit is outside the admitted grammar. Use a plain feature-branch commit or an exact absolute-target commit in that fresh invocation; an admitted switch or literal cd may participate only under the stated grammar.

Worktree identity and terminal full symbolic HEAD are established by scrubbed, bounded read-only probes. Alternate paths to one Git directory share conditional branch state; linked worktrees retain separate HEAD state. Existing switch destinations must be validated local branches, without symbolic-alias or remote-guess ambiguity. Probe failures, malformed output, timeouts, and exhausted input/output/evaluation budgets withhold proof. Literal detection examines decoded and raw unclassified segments independently of ordinary Git segments; admitted literal message/printf data is not executable syntax. This finite grammar and literal detector do not discover every commit hidden behind renamed executables, aliases, functions, opaque scripts, or unparseable fragmentation. Other tools and commit-producing verbs such as merge, cherry-pick, revert, am, and rebase remain outside this direct-commit boundary.

TRUST ASSUMPTIONS: trusted executable/builtin resolution; correspondence between the hook and execution environments; stable paths and configuration; and non-hostile hooks, editors, and helpers. Concurrent changes and probe-to-execution races remain residual risks. Server-side protection is a separate layer and does not validate this local pre-execution proof.

PUSH COVERAGE REMAINS SEPARATE. A raw-text backstop scans every submitted command unstripped, before any parsing, one command segment at a time (backslash-newline continuations are joined first, as bash joins them, then the text is split at newlines and at ;, &, | separators outside provable quoting, a # opening a comment only where bash starts a word; an unterminated construct leaves the remainder one segment), reads each segment as written, with its line continuations joined, and with quotes, a $ before a quote, and backslashes removed, and denies when one segment pairs a git push with a force, delete, mirror or --all/--branches sweep spelling and a protected branch name. Each of those long options is matched at every abbreviation git 2.55 accepts as unambiguous, derived from the long-option set of git push: --force, --force-w for --force-with-lease, --force-i for --force-if-includes, --m for --mirror, --al for --all, --b for --branches, --de for --delete and --pru for --prune (the shorter --for and --forc, which git rejects as ambiguous, match too); push-shaped prose pairing those inside one segment, in a heredoc body line, quoted string, comment or commit message, is denied too, a disclosed over-denial in the safe direction, while a force spelling, deletion flag, protected name or option value that appears only in a different segment (a rebase onto origin/main beside a feature force-push, an rm -rf beside a plain push, a --format or --depth value) does not pair. Commit-free commands retain the existing lexical push classifier: force and protected deletion deny; an unprovable sweep or apparent force/delete denies fail-safe. Force includes short clusters, conservative long prefixes, leases, --force-if-includes, --mirror, and + refspecs. Sweeps include forced --all/--branches, matching :/+:, wildcard force/deletion, and --prune with wildcard/matching refspecs or --all/--branches. Operand roles distinguish the repository from destination refspecs; supported value-taking options and --/--end-of-options are consumed before flags and destinations are judged. Command-local remote.<name>.mirror configuration via separated -c is value-aware and last-value-wins for a direct same-key assignment; --config-env for that key denies regardless of the unread environment value. A refspec-less force or a forced/deleted HEAD/@ uses the separate scrubbed session-HEAD probe; unknown HEAD or an unresolved repository view denies. Deleted HEAD/@ are conservatively denied even though Git can reject those delete spellings. Plain non-force pushes and explicit non-protected destinations can allow.

Push residuals include execution outside Bash; renamed executables, aliases, functions, and scripts; runtime-expanded destinations; fragmentation beyond parsed, raw and de-quoted detection (such as an escape decoded inside an ANSI-C quote); a wrapped force, delete, mirror or --all/--branches push naming no protected branch when another earlier or later segment parses as ordinary Git and suppresses the broad push fallback (one pairing a protected branch name with a force, delete, mirror or sweep spelling in the same segment is caught by the raw-text backstop, including a spelling fragmented by quotes or a backslash under a command-word wrapper); protected branches under names other than main/master; remote-side or hosting-provider actions; persisted repository/worktree/global/system configuration and includes; command-local remote.<name>.push refspecs; environment GIT_CONFIG_* protocols, including the explicit-refspec ambient-override gap; and upstream/triangular mappings that can diverge from the session-HEAD proxy. push.default selects refs rather than forcing or deleting by itself. The raw mirror-config fallback recognizes common quoted spellings but cannot model arbitrary option/key/value fragmentation or cross-mechanism precedence. The abbreviation match follows the recorded git 2.55 push option set: an abbreviation that a later git accepts because it drops or renames a push option is not matched until that recorded set is updated, and --tags and --follow-tags are not matched (they add tags and never update or delete a branch). Negated force/delete flags, standalone --force-if-includes, and dry-run force/delete can over-deny. Parse-error/raw fallback scans and the raw-text backstop can also over-match quoted prose or unrelated option values that share a segment with a push; the push fallback scans the RAW command text with NO heredoc stripping at all (stripping removes text, so any stripping defect can only hide a live push - an earlier stripper still erased a real force-push behind a stacked heredoc and behind a quoted-heredoc lookalike nested in quotes inside a command substitution), so force-push-shaped prose inside ANY heredoc body, quoted bodies included, can over-deny on this fallback path, including prose naming only a feature ref when the command is unparseable or wrapper-hidden; the backstop reads the heredoc body lines, quoted strings and comments inside a segment as text. When the shell reading is uncertain (any unquoted #, <<, ( or ), a lone { or } word, any backtick or $(, a line continuation the lexer reads differently once joined, or a form the lexer refuses), the broad fallback decides even beside an ordinary Git segment and reads the text both as written and with quotes, a $ before a quote, and backslashes removed, so a force, delete or mirror spelling anywhere in such a command denies, including a force-push to a feature branch inside a subshell, inside a { } brace group beside another Git command, beside a command substitution, or carrying a # inside a word: a disclosed over-denial in the safe direction. Push coverage is best-effort and is not widened by the commit certificates.

DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took 0.75 to 0.87 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 that was running other work (runs on 2026-10-17; which clock those runs read, CPU or wall-clock time, was not recorded), because the raw-text push backstop reads the whole command, one segment at a time, before the 65,536-character size cap of the commit reading denies a longer one. Those shapes now include two that were measured separately, on 2026-10-18: a run of quoted '-c' mirror options with no blank, and a run of adjacent '<(' or '>(' process substitutions, each before a force-push to a protected branch. While the backstop read the first with the single mirror-configuration regex, whose cost grew with the square of the run's length, one call of this check on it took 14.0 s of CPU time at 256 KB and reached no decision within the 60-second hang guard of the hooks self-test at 1 MB; with the linear probe that replaced that regex, it took at most 0.47 s of CPU time at 1 MB. On the second, which the backstop's segment split now walks in place instead of copying the rest of the command for each substitution, it took about 0.17 s of CPU time at 1 MB. Each figure was measured in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4. Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

gates.residue: Judges only the revision under gate against the derived protected ref: it does not scan the repository's other branches, cannot prove where a branch was originally cut (a branch cut from a sibling that itself descends from the protected line still resolves), passes a fork point that survives a partial rewrite unless the configured lag threshold catches it, does not fail on multiple merge bases, and where no threshold is configured the staleness layer reports and never blocks. With multiple merge bases the reported first-parent lag is the MINIMUM (most-lenient) across bases, so a criss-cross history is judged by its nearest fork point. Replace refs are neutralized in the scrubbed env (GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1) so a `git replace --graft` cannot mask an orphan as rooted through merge-base; the on-disk .git/info/grafts residual is out of scope (an accidental-case guardrail; full adversarial-grade parent-rewrite resistance is not this gate's remit). A shallow repository maps a merge-base miss to cannot-evaluate (exit 2) with a `git fetch --unshallow` remediation, never a false ORPHANED, because truncated history cannot be told from a genuinely absent root (the CI gate checks out at fetch-depth:0). When the protected ref is derived from the default origin/HEAD, a stale local origin/HEAD (not refreshed since the last fetch) can skew the derived protected tip, so both the orphaned and the first-parent-lag verdicts are only as current as the clone's remote-tracking state; pass --protected an authoritative ref, or refresh origin/HEAD, when that currency matters. A degenerate invocation naming the SAME ref for --protected and --head is a self-comparison that always resolves (a ref is rooted on itself); the caller supplies distinct refs. The gate scrubs the ambient GIT_* environment before every git call but resolves the `git` executable through the ambient PATH, so it trusts the toolchain's `git`; a hostile PATH entry shadowing `git` is a trusted-toolchain / execution-environment concern outside this gate's threat model, not a branch-root bypass it defends against.

hooks.residue: Lexical trigger over an open command grammar. NO-ASK posture: this guard never returns an ask; branch rooting is a hazard class, so read every ASK, fail-SAFE ASK, and routes-to-ASK below as a DENY-and-educate fail-safe (a confirmed orphan start and any creation form this guard cannot prove rooted both DENY, naming the reachable correct action; the authoritative CI branch-root gate judges the actual post-creation ancestry). A branch created through a wrapper, alias, script, or shell indirection is not seen. When a later construct makes the whole command unparseable (a heredoc, a process substitution), the guard still PARTIAL-lexes and judges the creation recovered in the parseable prefix, so a proven orphan creation followed by an unsupported construct still DENIES (DENY outranks the parse error); only a creation lying ENTIRELY within the unparseable syntax stays unseen (the open-grammar residual), and only creation forms are checked, so switching to an existing orphaned branch, continuing work on the current branch, or RENAMING a branch (-m/-M/--move, which reuses an existing branch's commits under a new name and so creates no new orphan-rootable ref) passes to the CI gate. It probes a creation's ancestry (and can DENY an orphaned start) ONLY for a CLEAN canonical creation: a create trigger (checkout -b/-B; switch -c/-C or --create/--force-create; a bare `git branch <name>`; a `git branch -c/-C/--copy` copy whose start is the SOURCE, an explicit <src> else the current HEAD; or `git worktree add -b/-B`), its operands, and NOTHING ELSE except a tiny allowlist of VALUELESS booleans (--quiet/--force, short q/f; git branch additionally exposes --verbose/-v, which checkout/switch/worktree do not). A confidently-recognized non-creation ACTION (git branch -d/-D/--delete, -m/-M/--move rename, -u/--set-upstream-to/--unset-upstream, --edit-description, --show-current) or a LISTING form (--list, -a/-r/--all/--remotes and the unambiguous listing letters) is ALLOWED. EVERY OTHER shape routes to a fail-SAFE ASK, never a silent allow of a possible creation and never a probe-based DENY of a non-creation: any value-taking option (--contains/--merged/--points-at/--recurse-submodules), any unknown option, any abbreviated (--cre, --orp, --tr) or negated form whose meaning is order- or version-dependent (--no-detach, `--list --no-list`, a clustered -l), any tracking/orphan/detach form (--track/-t/--orphan/--guess/--detach/-d), a copy combined with any non-clean option (git branch --format main -c ...), a bare `git worktree add <path> [<commit-ish>]` without -b, and any short cluster carrying a letter outside the clean/listing set. This MAXIMALLY-CONSERVATIVE posture (maintainer-approved 2026-09-02, after the simplify-to-ASK cap) trades precision for robustness: an exotic or option-laden git command earns an ASK rather than a precise allow or deny, and the authoritative CI branch-root gate judges the actual post-creation ancestry regardless. DISCLOSED residual: the classifier accepts any nonempty operand as a branch name, so a creation carrying a git-INVALID name (spaces, a `..`, a control character - forms git rejects with `check-ref-format` and creates nothing) can still receive a probe-based deny of that orphaned start; this is a safe-direction false-deny of a no-op command (re-issue with a valid name), and full git ref-name validation is out of this lexical classifier's scope (tracked as HYG-2). What it PROVES at creation time is only that the start point is ORPHANED (no merge base with origin/HEAD); a rooted-but-STALE or old start point (for example checkout -b x origin/HEAD~1) still has a merge base and PASSES this hook, and its staleness is caught only by the CI gate's configured --max-lag first-parent-lag threshold, not here. Replace refs are neutralized on the probe (GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1) so a grafted parent cannot make an orphan look rooted; the on-disk .git/info/grafts residual is out of scope (an accidental-case guardrail). A shallow clone cannot distinguish a missing merge base from unfetched history, so a merge-base miss in a shallow repository routes to ASK, never a deny; a FAILURE of the shallow-status probe itself (a non-zero or unreadable result) likewise routes to ASK, matching the CI gate's cannot-evaluate posture, never a false orphaned deny. A cd/pushd in an earlier segment of the compound command or a non-cosmetic ambient GIT_* variable leaves the target repository unreconcilable with the session cwd, so the creation routes to a fail-safe deny. A command-local redirect is resolved to the REPOSITORY the branch is created in and its ancestry probed THERE: a resolvable -C target is probed, and --work-tree is worktree-only so the repository is resolved from -C or the ambient cwd, never from the --work-tree value (a review finding); only a --git-dir/GIT_DIR/-c form or an unresolvable -C target cannot be pinned and allow-notes (the CI branch-root gate remains the backstop). The ancestry answer comes from the clone's remote-tracking state, which can be stale until the next fetch. The hook derives its PROTECTED ref from the clone's origin/HEAD (the local default-branch pointer), which may differ from the actual protected target the CI gate judges against (the PR base branch): where origin/HEAD points at a non-default branch, the hook can ALLOW a creation the CI gate later reports ORPHANED against the true protected line, since the hook has no PR/target context at creation time; the CI branch-root gate is the authoritative check on the actual post-creation ancestry. The hook resolves the `git` executable through the ambient PATH (a trusted-toolchain boundary, as the sibling gate residue discloses): a hostile PATH entry shadowing `git` could spoof the probe, an adversarial execution-environment concern outside this accidental-case hook's threat model, not a bypass it defends against. The env-assignment command form is best-effort, as for the sibling git hooks. The hook catches only EXPLICIT-start creation forms; an IMPLICIT-start (DWIM) form where git auto-creates a branch from a matching remote-tracking ref (a bare git checkout/switch <name> whose name matches a remote branch, or a --guess/--guess-remote guess) has a start git resolves at runtime and not lexically visible here, so it is routed to ASK where a guess flag is present and otherwise passes the hook and is caught by the authoritative CI branch-root gate, which judges the actual post-creation ancestry. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 1.35 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

gates.residue: Total over its declared surface: every Python script the local check roster launches and every runner the self-test execution manifest registers. Each must parse from its raw bytes and carry exactly one top-level test of the bare name __name__ against the exact string "__main__", as its last top-level statement, with no else, whose body ends in a call statement (an expression statement whose value is a call, or raise SystemExit of a call) with no raise anywhere before it in that body (at any depth, and conservatively inside a definition too); a deleted, duplicated, displaced, nested, misnamed, misspelled, or empty entry, and one whose only call is dormant (inside a definition, a lambda, a nested branch, or a try) or follows a raise, always fails. Every control input (the roster, the manifest, and each script) is opened non-blocking without following a final symlink and must be a regular file: a missing, unreadable, or unparsable script, a symlink, FIFO, directory, or other non-regular path, an unreadable, malformed, or schema-invalid roster or manifest (the manifest is held to the execution gate's own schema validator), and a roster that launches no Python script cannot be evaluated (exit 2). No gate can hold its own entry (with its guard lost, both of its steps exit 0 silently), so its self-test is registered as the suite entry-guard-selftest and both rosters launch it only through the execution gate, which reads the missing execution report of a child that ran nothing as cannot-evaluate (exit 2); the self-test reproduces this on a scratch copy with its own guard deleted, and launches its own live step as a child and requires its PASS line. That holds only while its registry row and both suite roster lines stay; a coordinated removal of them is outside it. It proves only that the entry exists in that form. A static check cannot see a neutralization that keeps that form: the final call running something that does not reach the checks or exiting with a constant status (sys.exit(0), print(), a bare main() whose failure status is dropped); an earlier statement in the guard body that exits or raises through a call, rebinds the called name (main = lambda: 0), or replaces the exit function (sys.exit = print); a top-level statement before the guard that exits, raises, or never returns (raise SystemExit(0), sys.exit, os._exit, an endless loop), rebinds __name__, rebinds or shadows the called name, or registers a hook that overrides the exit status (atexit.register(os._exit, 0), a signal handler, sys.excepthook); an import whose side effect exits or replaces sys.exit or a builtin; a dispatch or check deleted inside a function the entry calls, which is caught for a registered suite only by the execution gate; and any other statement that changes control flow or the exit status before or during the final call. A symlinked parent directory is followed. It does not read the CI workflow (the parity gate holds the two rosters equal), does not see a script the roster never launches, and cannot tell a legitimate from an illegitimate coordinated removal of an entry and its roster line in one reviewed change. Its self-test proves each vector discriminating against its own table of single-check removal mutants, not against every possible regression, and the execution gate accounts for its checks by family (every vector, every mutant, each launch leg), not per vector.

Total over its declared surface, in three layers. Layer one, STATIC pre-launch: every check() call site in the registered runner's source is resolved to literal ids and that set must equal the hand-authored expectation manifest tools/selftest_checks.toml exactly before any child is launched; it resolves only direct bare-name check() call sites with string-literal or for-loop-literal ids (the loop attribution is the innermost enclosing for, lexical only: it does not model any intervening dataflow between the loop header and the call site, a rebinding of the loop variable or a nested function boundary, so such a site can mis-attribute its ids, caught, if at all, by the runtime set reconcile), and a non-call reference to the bare name check, a comprehension-bound id Name, any other unresolvable or duplicate source id, and source that does not parse are refused fail-closed, never silently resolved, while two static blind spots remain, bounded the same way: an invocation route the static layer never sees a call site for because it never names check as a bare Name in Load context (getattr, exec, an import that binds a different name and is then called through it, or a globals()['check'] lookup), and a rebinding of the name check the static layer cannot detect (any Store-class or non-Load binding: an assignment, a with-as or except-as target, a nested def check or class check, an import check, a del check, or a global or nonlocal declaration), which leaves the direct call sites visible and counted while they may no longer invoke the instrumented helper; both are caught, if at all, by the runtime set reconcile, a registered id whose only route is invisible (no direct call site at all) is refused by the static layer pre-launch as a registered id with no source check(), and the dead-direct-site decoy (a route that re-executes an already-registered id whose direct call site is dead) passes both set layers and is bounded only by the non-discrimination residual (a constant-true check counts as executed). Layer two, RUNTIME: the executed check-id set recorded at the instrumented check() choke point is emitted as a strict structured report and reconciled exactly against the same manifest, judged with the child's real exit code; missing, extra, or duplicate ids, a missing, malformed, wrong-suite, or non-regular report, a malformed manifest, and every cannot-evaluate fail closed, and a child exit 0 never overrides a missing or mismatched report. Layer three: the child carries its own in-run self-guard, reconciling the same set even on a direct developer run of an intact runner; the self-guard sits behind the runner's module entry, so it cannot fire once that entry is gone (the runner then exits 0 with no output and no report on a direct run, which this gate reports as cannot-evaluate only when it launches the runner itself), and the entry-guard gate holds that entry in place for every registered runner. The child suite's own behavioural assurance (the orchestrator-integrity acceptance vectors over hermetic fixtures, judged on structured verdicts) rides the child's verdict, which this gate requires; the gate launches that child under a git-neutral environment built in two layers (HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME pinned to a fresh empty directory, so the per-user global config, ignore, and attributes surfaces are empty for every descendant git call, including one made after a descendant scrubs the GIT_* environment and drops the GIT_* pins, plus, for the immediate child, ambient GIT_* dropped, the global and system config files pinned to os.devnull with GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM, and core.excludesFile and core.attributesFile overridden to os.devnull by injected entries), and drops every ambient PYTHON*-prefixed variable from the child environment, transitively neutralizing PYTHONPATH/sitecustomize module injection into descendant interpreters (nothing downstream re-derives or re-sets a PYTHON* variable, and the runner's own interpreter grandchild launches carry -I -B as defence in depth for a direct developer run), which hardens the GATE-launched child only, the runner's own direct-invocation hermeticity being a separately tracked item; three launch-environment bounds are disclosed: the system-wide git config ($(prefix)/etc/gitconfig) is neutralized only for the immediate child (GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM and the GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM pin are themselves GIT_-prefixed, so a scrubbing descendant drops them) and the system-wide attributes file ($(prefix)/etc/gitattributes) is not neutralized at all (no GIT_ATTR_NOSYSTEM is injected, and a scrubbing descendant would drop it the same way), a hostile system-wide file being root-owned, the same trust tier as the git binary itself and so at the threat-model boundary, outside what this gate defends, and git is resolved through the ambient PATH, a trusted-toolchain concern outside this gate's threat model, and the environment drop neutralizes the PYTHON*-prefixed family only, a loader-level injection control such as LD_PRELOAD and the interpreter binary itself sitting at the same trusted-toolchain tier, outside this gate's threat model. It proves SET IDENTITY AND EXECUTION only: it does not prove an invoked assertion is discriminating (a constant-true check counts as executed), carries no mutation sensitivity, sees nothing outside the instrumented check() helper (an assertion made by a direct FAILURES.append outside the choke point, whose non-execution is invisible to the execution set, a direct EXECUTED.append or _EXECUTED_SET.add that manufactures execution evidence for a check that never really ran, or a suite not registered), and cannot distinguish a legitimate from an illegitimate coordinated deletion of a check and its manifest row in one reviewed change. The static scan and the launch read the runner's source at two moments, so a concurrent same-user writer between them is outside this repo's sole-orchestrator threat model (the runtime layer still reconciles what actually ran); repo-root confirmation is a .git-existence proxy anchored to the gate's own file, not a full git-identity check; and the expectation manifest is trusted hand-authored input whose schema is machine-validated but whose completeness rests on source review. A row may carry an optional args list of literal arguments, forwarded to the runner ahead of the gate's own --execution-report pair; each must be a string of at most 200 characters from a closed printable-ASCII set (a letter or digit first, or one or two dashes and then one), and an argument that names, abbreviates, or attaches a value to --execution-report is refused, while any other shape is refused too. The filter is lexical: no row can redirect the report through the named option, and nothing more is claimed about what an accepted argument means to a given runner; a runner that writes no report (one that stops parsing, exits early, or takes the rest of its argv as data) is a missing report, cannot-evaluate, never a pass. Rows whose runners resolve to one path form a group: before any launch, every row of the requested suite's group must carry args no other row of the group carries, the rows' expected sets must be pairwise disjoint, and their union must equal the runner's static check() set exactly; a gap, an overlap, an extra id, or a missing or repeated args list is cannot-evaluate, and a single-row runner is held to the whole set exactly as before. Membership resolves every row's runner strictly, so a missing path, a non-directory component, a symlink loop or a permission error in any row's runner is cannot-evaluate before any report directory is allocated or any runner launched, never an assumed non-member, a runner path carrying a control or format character (C0, DEL, C1, the bidi controls, U+2028 and U+2029) is refused by the schema, and a suite id outside the closed suite-id grammar (a letter or digit first, then letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-' only) is refused by name, so a space-joined launch identity can never stand for a registered suite. Before any launch, every registered row must also have its launch line (check_selftest_execution.py --suite <id>) in both tools/run_all_checks.sh and .github/workflows/quality.yml, each read as a regular file through the parity gate's validated loader; a missing, non-regular, unreadable or loader-rejected roster, or a row whose launch line is missing from at least one of the two, is cannot-evaluate; a roster member counts as a launch line only when it is exactly check_selftest_execution.py --suite <id>, the one argv shape the gate's command line accepts, so a member carrying any further argument, or a near-miss id, launches nothing. That check is lexical: it proves each launch line is present, not that it runs or passes. The group rule is checked for the requested suite's group only, once per invocation, and launches that one row, so that every other row is launched rests on the lexical launch-line check; nor does the group rule prove that the runner's handling of its args selects the declared subset other than through the runtime reconcile of the row actually launched; a runner reached through a hard link or a byte copy under another path forms its own group, held alone to the whole static set, so an undetected group member can only be refused, never pass with a subset. Registered surface at this release: the orch-behaviour-selftest, ci-status-behaviour-selftest, git-fixture-env-core, git-fixture-env-config-combined, git-fixture-env-config-malformed, git-fixture-env-config-system, instruction-budget-selftest, python-floor-selftest, entry-guard-selftest, brief-capability-selftest, and hook-latency-selftest suites.

Total over the surface it examines: an OPEN merge_pending row carrying a TYPED ref (pr:N, decision:X) whose merge or record evidence exists in the declared truth sources always fails the gate. It reads only typed structured refs; a narrative number in prose, an untyped row, or a register kept outside the declared surface is out of scope by design (D9), and drift the truth sources themselves cannot see (an unpushed local merge, a PR merged under a subject with no (#N) marker) passes. In a checkout with no orchestration registry the live leg is NOT APPLICABLE (the record is machine-local by design) and the self-test carries the assurance; that scope boundary is printed, never silent.

hooks.residue: A best-effort QUOTE-AWARE LEXICAL check over the Bash command string: tokenized with the shared quote/redirect-aware tokenizer (_lex_command), which respects quotes and REMOVES shell redirection from the token stream (so a redirect before or around the subcommand no longer hides a Co-Authored-By trailer, an --author value, or an identity assignment), reading bash locale quoting ($"...") as the double-quoted text bash reads when no message catalogue translates it, so a name that $"" splits inside a word is read joined (Cl$""aude is Claude) in the command and in each run line it reads, and grouped into segments on the unquoted shell operators ; | || && & ( ) and newlines, so a subshell-grouped commit (( git commit --author=... )) is judged too, and a trailer hiding inside a quoted -m message (-m "fix; Co-authored-by: Claude", which the old whitespace split broke at the ;) now lives intact in the single message token and is caught by a substring scan on that token. Each command and each run line is judged under two readings, the one above and one that keeps the $ of a locale quote as a literal character, as the tokenizer reads it for every other guard, and an AI identity that either reading finds denies: a name followed directly by a locale quote (Claude$"bot", which bash reads as Claudebot, a word that names no AI identity) still denies as it did before locale quoting was read, because a change toward allow is held until the maintainer decides it. A command or run line that only one reading can parse (a {$"x"}> word, which the locale reading takes for an fd-variable redirect) is judged under that reading. The run lines that each reading alone builds are read within a length bound kept for that reading, and those that only a mix of the two readings builds within a third (each the length bound below), so the lines that one reading does not build cannot spend the bound of the lines it reads alone, and a line past the bound of one reading is left unread even when the other reading reads it; the cost is up to three bounds of run lines rather than one, and a line holding $" is tokenized under both readings. On a git commit-family segment (commit, merge, cherry-pick, am, rebase, revert, commit-tree) it flags a Co-Authored-By trailer inside a token (every trailer name in the token is read, each with its own value of up to 160 characters to the end of its line, so a second trailer on the same line inside the value of the first, or one on a later line of the message, is judged too) or an --author value (--author=X or --author X) naming an AI; in ANY segment it flags a git-identity env var (GIT_AUTHOR_NAME/GIT_COMMITTER_NAME) or a user.name/user.email value (a -c user.name=X inline or a config user.name X pair) naming an AI, so setting the identity in a prior segment then committing is caught. The commit-family contexts are read on a segment whose git command has a commit-family subcommand, and the git command is found after leading shell reserved words (!, if, then, do, a { group and the rest), the NAME after function or coproc when a compound command follows it (function f { git commit ...; }, coproc C { git commit ...; }; coproc C env git ... runs C) and VAR=value words: the command word itself when it is git (a path to git included), and, when the command word is one of the wrappers env, timeout, command, exec, nohup, xargs, sudo, nice, setsid, stdbuf or time, a later word that is git (a path to git included, a VAR=value word excluded) starts a candidate git command, whatever options and operands the wrapper carries (env git commit, sudo -u ci git commit, sudo -u git git commit, timeout -s KILL 60 git commit, nested wrappers too), until a held candidate, whose git word does not stand right after a word that may be an option taking it as a value (a word starting with - other than -, -- or an option carrying =), has a subcommand that is a git command name (a git 2.55 built-in or listed command): that candidate is taken to be the git command the segment runs and a later git word is its operand, so a wrapped read-side command with a git-named operand allows (env git log --grep git commit --author=...), while a held candidate whose subcommand is not a git command name, such as a git-named operand of a program off the wrapper list, leaves later git words read (sudo flock /var/lock/git env git commit, sudo chroot /srv/git /usr/bin/env git commit); all of this in one pass over the words of the segment; command -v and command -V (a command whose options carry v or V) only look a name up and run no git command. A command that git runs from its own operands is read as a command line of its own, bare or wrapped: the operands of git submodule foreach and of git submodule--helper foreach, to which git submodule foreach hands them (its first operand, after an optional --, is shell text and the rest are its arguments, so foreach git commit ... and foreach "git commit ..." both run git commit), and of git bisect run (the words of one command), and the value of git rebase --exec or -x in any spelling git accepts (-x CMD, -xCMD, -ix CMD, --exec=CMD, --ex CMD), a shell command line; such lines are read nested up to 8 deep and up to 8 times the length of the command plus 4096 characters in all, and each git rebase reads its options only up to the next rebase subcommand of its segment, from where that rebase finds the same lines, so a segment of many wrapped rebase commands costs time linear in its length. A line past either bound is left unread, and so is a run line at any depth that the shared tokenizer cannot parse (an unbalanced quote in a foreach operand or an exec value), but every other segment of the command and of each line being read, and every other run line within the bounds, is still judged, so an AI identity there denies. Only when none sets one does the fallback judge the whole command. It first denies when an AI identity appears anywhere in the command once every backslash-newline, backslash and quote is removed, so quoting or escaping in the unread line that splits or builds an option name or value (--"auth"=..., --author=C"laude ...", a backslash-newline before the value) does not hide it, or once the $ before each double quote is removed as well, so locale quoting in the unread line (--author=Cl$""aude ...) does not hide it either, and otherwise the raw-string scan below still judges it; the cost is a safe-direction over-deny of such a command (a nest past a bound, or a run line that cannot be parsed) whose text merely names an AI product (-m "fix claude adapter", a read-side git log --author=..., a word in a quoted heredoc body). An identity the shell builds at run time in the unread line (an expansion, a command substitution, or ANSI-C quoting) is not seen, and on any line neither is the text that a message catalogue substitutes for a locale quote at run time. The cost of that one bounded wrapper rule is a safe-direction over-deny when a wrapped command that is not git carries git, a commit verb and an AI identity as its own operands (xargs echo git commit --author=...), when a wrapped read-side git word stands right after a wrapper option (sudo -E git log --grep git commit --author=...), when a wrapped read-side git command has an alias as its subcommand (env git lg --grep git commit --author=...), or when a command -v lookup stands behind another wrapper (sudo command -v git commit --author=...). Each word is read as a git commit option the way git 2.55 parses its options, so the value of a value-taking option is read as that value, never as an --author option (git commit -m --author=X and git commit -am --author=X record a message, not an author). One exception is kept: a next-word value of any value-taking option, in any spelling read below (-m, -F, -C, -c, -t, -U, --trailer, --date, --fixup, --squash, --template, --cleanup, --pathspec-from-file, --reuse-message, --reedit-message, --unified, --inter-hunk-context and --author itself), that has the form --author=VALUE naming an AI identity still denies as an --author value, and so does the word after a next-word value that is --author or a prefix git reads as --author (git commit -m --author X, git commit -m --auth X) when that word names an AI identity, bare, behind a wrapper word or in a run line; git takes the value word as that option value and records no author from it, so this is a safe-direction over-deny over every value-taking option, which the maintainer chose to keep (the wrapped and run-line forms, and the word after a prefix such as --auth, were allowed before wrapped commands, run lines and abbreviations were read, so denying them is stricter still). A value that shares its option word (-m--author=X, --message=--author=X) and a next-word value of the form --auth=X (a prefix shorter than --author, with =) are not so judged. A short option cluster is read letter by letter up to its first value-taking letter (m, F, C, c, t, U), whose value is the rest of the word or else the next word and only that word (git commit -am -m --author=X records the message -m and the author X), -S and -u take a value only from the rest of their own word, and a long option is matched by its exact name or by a prefix that only one git commit option starts with (--auth is --author, --mess is --message; a prefix that several options share takes no value, and git refuses it). A message value (-m, --message, --trailer) is still scanned for a co-author trailer, and the value of a file, commit, template, date, mode or number option (-F or --file, -C or --reuse-message, -c or --reedit-message, -t or --template, -U or --unified, --fixup, --squash, --date, --cleanup, --pathspec-from-file, --inter-hunk-context) is passed over. The other commit-family verbs are read with the same git commit option table, not their own. git global options that take an argument (-C, -c, --git-dir, --work-tree, --namespace, --exec-path, --super-prefix, --config-env), whose value is now its own token, are skipped so the value is not misread as the subcommand. The BARE message body is deliberately NOT matched against the identity set: a legitimate message that merely mentions an AI product name (-m "fix claude adapter") records no AI identity, and denying it would be a false positive; only a trailer or an --author value records identity. On a shell parse error (unbalanced quotes) in the command itself, with a run line left unread (one that cannot be parsed or one past the run-line bounds) and nothing read setting an AI identity, or with a command too long to read (below) that names an AI and holds no word that can record an identity, it fails SAFE: a conservative raw-string scan denies an apparent AI trailer/--author/env/config assignment, never a silent-allow; its --author context is every prefix git reads as --author (--au, --aut, --auth, --autho, --author) with = or whitespace before the value, and its co-author context reads every trailer name, as the reader does, and takes each whitespace run whole, so a long run of newlines after the trailer name costs time linear in its length rather than quadratic, with the same AI identities found, and so does its user.name/user.email context, so a long run of spaces after user.name before a quote that does not close costs time linear in its length too, with the same values found. A command longer than 131,072 characters is not read at all, so the reading ends well inside the 10-second hook timeout, which the platform contract this repository records does not say refuses a call when it runs out (the costliest commands measured took up to about 7.3 microseconds of CPU time per character to read, about 1 s at that length, which holds only while each regex the reader runs on a word, and each one the raw-string scan runs on a command of that length that the tokenizer cannot parse, costs time linear in the length it scans: the co-author trailer regex the reader runs on each word takes each whitespace run whole, as the co-author and user.name/user.email contexts of the raw-string scan do, since giving a run back one character at a time cost time quadratic in its length, about 53 s and 130 s of CPU time at that length for a commit message of a trailer name and a run of newlines and for user.name and a run of spaces before a quote that does not close, against about 0.01 s with each run taken whole, and a commit message of repeated trailer names, each read with its own value, in git rebase -x lines nested seven deep, the innermost ending in a locale quote, took up to about 0.15 s, against 0.41 s with each value searched whole): such a command is denied when an AI name appears anywhere in it once every quote, backslash, $ and newline is removed, with no word boundary needed around the name, and it also holds a word that can record an identity: git as a whole word (its letters with only quotes, backslashes, $ signs or newlines between them, and no letter, digit or underscore directly before or after it, a removed character counting as a word boundary, so a git at the start of a line is found), or a GIT_AUTHOR_ or GIT_COMMITTER_ variable name or user.name or user.email in any case once those characters are removed. Any other command that long that names an AI is judged by the conservative raw-string scan above, as one that cannot be parsed is, so an AI co-author trailer or --author value in it denies even when git runs under another name (gi? or "$G"), and one that names no AI is allowed at once, since that scan cannot find an AI identity in it either. This fallback has no length bound, so its own cost grows with the command length: on the costliest shapes measured, commands made of repeated co-author trailer names, each read with its own value of up to 160 characters, of which the AI identity search reads only the part past the end of the value before it, less 8 characters (the longest AI name the check matches between word boundaries, 9 characters, less one), the highest of three single runs on one host took about 0.26 s of CPU time at 1,048,576 characters, 4.0 s at 16,777,216 and 6.3 s at 25,165,824 (with each value searched whole, 0.59 s, 8.7 s and 14.0 s on the same host), and 7.3 s at 33,554,432, 8.9 s at 41,943,040 and 10.3 s at 50,331,648, so on the measuring host a command of about 40 to 48 MiB or longer can outlast the 10-second hook timeout, and on a slower host a shorter one can; since the platform contract this repository records does not say that a hook stopped at its timeout refuses the call, such a command may run with no deny from this check. The reader finds a git command only by a word that is git or a path ending in /git, reads a run line only under such a git command, and judges an identity assignment only in a word that starts with one of those names, so a name and a word that the reader would find in the command are found by these scans as well; a command that runs git under another name (a variable, a function or an alias) is outside the reader too. The cost is a safe-direction over-deny of such a long command whose text merely names an AI product or holds an AI name inside a longer word (Claudette) and holds git as a word or one of those names, a quoted heredoc body included; a long command that names an AI product and holds none of those words (a heredoc that writes a file and runs no git) is allowed unless the raw-string scan finds an AI co-author trailer, --author value or identity assignment in it, which denies it even when that is only text the heredoc writes, the same safe-direction over-deny as on a parse error. Being a raw-string scan, on a parse error in the command itself it does not see an option name or value that shell quoting or escaping splits or builds (--"auth"=..., --author=C"laude ...", --author=Cl$""aude ..., a backslash-newline before the value); with a run line left unread the scan for an AI identity anywhere, above, covers those forms. It is BEST-EFFORT: it targets the common/accidental case (the assistant own accidental violation), not an adversary determined to evade it. It does NOT defeat deliberate shell escaping (git \commit), obfuscation, an alias or function that renames the tool, a wrapper outside that list (builtin, doas, ionice, chrt, taskset, flock, busybox, watch, script, a wrapper script), a command string a shell or wrapper parses at run time (sh -c, bash -c, eval, env -S or --split-string with a quoted command), an identity a wrapper reads at run time (arguments xargs reads from its input), a git word built at run time (an expansion such as $GIT), a command git runs from somewhere other than the operands above (the exec lines of an interactive rebase todo list, git for-each-repo, an alias that starts with !, a configured editor, a filter-branch filter, or another git option or config value that names a program), a git-named operand of a program off the wrapper list followed by a word spelled as a git command name (sudo chroot /srv/git init ...), or persistent shell/env/config state such as an AI identity persisted in git config in a PRIOR TURN (not the same command), a trailer staged into a message file and committed with -F/-t, a commit made outside the Bash tool or the session, or an AI product name outside the recognized identity set. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 0.10 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (three runs on 2026-10-16; a command past the 131,072-character read bound goes straight to the fallback).
