Probe failures, malformed output, timeouts, and exhausted input/output/evaluation budgets withhold proof. Literal detection examines decoded and raw unclassified segments independently of ordinary Git segments; admitted literal message/printf data is not executable syntax. This finite grammar and literal detector do not discover every commit hidden behind renamed executables, aliases, functions, opaque scripts, or unparseable fragmentation. Other tools and commit-producing verbs such as merge, cherry-pick, revert, am, and rebase remain outside this direct-commit boundary.

TRUST ASSUMPTIONS: trusted executable/builtin resolution; correspondence between the hook and execution environments; stable paths and configuration; and non-hostile hooks, editors, and helpers. Concurrent changes and probe-to-execution races remain residual risks. Server-side protection is a separate layer and does not validate this local pre-execution proof.

PUSH COVERAGE REMAINS SEPARATE. A raw-text backstop scans every submitted command unstripped, before any parsing, one command segment at a time (backslash-newline continuations are joined first, as bash joins them, then the text is split at newlines and at ;, &, | separators outside provable quoting, a # opening a comment only where bash starts a word; an unterminated construct leaves the remainder one segment), reads each segment as written, with its line continuations joined, and with quotes, a $ before a quote, and backslashes removed, and denies when one segment pairs a git push with a force, delete, mirror or --all/--branches sweep spelling and a protected branch name. Each of those long options is matched at every abbreviation git 2.55 accepts as unambiguous, derived from the long-option set of git push: --force, --force-w for --force-with-lease, --force-i for --force-if-includes, --m for --mirror, --al for --all, --b for --branches, --de for --delete and --pru for --prune (the shorter --for and --forc, which git rejects as ambiguous, match too); push-shaped prose pairing those inside one segment, in a heredoc body line, quoted string, comment or commit message, is denied too, a disclosed over-denial in the safe direction, while a force spelling, deletion flag, protected name or option value that appears only in a different segment (a rebase onto origin/main beside a feature force-push, an rm -rf beside a plain push, a --format or --depth value) does not pair. Commit-free commands retain the existing lexical push classifier: force and protected deletion deny; an unprovable sweep or apparent force/delete denies fail-safe. Force includes short clusters, conservative long prefixes, leases, --force-if-includes, --mirror, and + refspecs. Sweeps include forced --all/--branches, matching :/+:, wildcard force/deletion, and --prune with wildcard/matching refspecs or --all/--branches. Operand roles distinguish the repository from destination refspecs; supported value-taking options and --/--end-of-options are consumed before flags and destinations are judged. Command-local remote.<name>.mirror configuration via separated -c is value-aware and last-value-wins for a direct same-key assignment; --config-env for that key denies regardless of the unread environment value. A refspec-less force or a forced/deleted HEAD/@ uses the separate scrubbed session-HEAD probe; unknown HEAD or an unresolved repository view denies. Deleted HEAD/@ are conservatively denied even though Git can reject those delete spellings. Plain non-force pushes and explicit non-protected destinations can allow.

Push residuals include execution outside Bash; renamed executables, aliases, functions, and scripts; runtime-expanded destinations; fragmentation beyond parsed, raw and de-quoted detection (such as an escape decoded inside an ANSI-C quote); a wrapped force, delete, mirror or --all/--branches push naming no protected branch when another earlier or later segment parses as ordinary Git and suppresses the broad push fallback (one pairing a protected branch name with a force, delete, mirror or sweep spelling in the same segment is caught by the raw-text backstop, including a spelling fragmented by quotes or a backslash under a command-word wrapper); protected branches under names other than main/master; remote-side or hosting-provider actions; persisted repository/worktree/global/system configuration and includes; command-local remote.<name>.push refspecs; environment GIT_CONFIG_* protocols, including the explicit-refspec ambient-override gap; and upstream/triangular mappings that can diverge from the session-HEAD proxy. push.default selects refs rather than forcing or deleting by itself. The raw mirror-config fallback recognizes common quoted spellings but cannot model arbitrary option/key/value fragmentation or cross-mechanism precedence. The abbreviation match follows the recorded git 2.55 push option set: an abbreviation that a later git accepts because it drops or renames a push option is not matched until that recorded set is updated, and --tags and --follow-tags are not matched (they add tags and never update or delete a branch). Negated force/delete flags, standalone --force-if-includes, and dry-run force/delete can over-deny. Parse-error/raw fallback scans and the raw-text backstop can also over-match quoted prose or unrelated option values that share a segment with a push; the push fallback scans the RAW command text with NO heredoc stripping at all (stripping removes text, so any stripping defect can only hide a live push - an earlier stripper still erased a real force-push behind a stacked heredoc and behind a quoted-heredoc lookalike nested in quotes inside a command substitution), so force-push-shaped prose inside ANY heredoc body, quoted bodies included, can over-deny on this fallback path, including prose naming only a feature ref when the command is unparseable or wrapper-hidden; the backstop reads the heredoc body lines, quoted strings and comments inside a segment as text. When the shell reading is uncertain (any unquoted #, <<, ( or ), a lone { or } word, any backtick or $(, a line continuation the lexer reads differently once joined, or a form the lexer refuses), the broad fallback decides even beside an ordinary Git segment and reads the text both as written and with quotes, a $ before a quote, and backslashes removed, so a force, delete or mirror spelling anywhere in such a command denies, including a force-push to a feature branch inside a subshell, inside a { } brace group beside another Git command, beside a command substitution, or carrying a # inside a word: a disclosed over-denial in the safe direction. Push coverage is best-effort and is not widened by the commit certificates.

DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took 0.75 to 0.87 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 that was running other work (runs on 2026-10-17; which clock those runs read, CPU or wall-clock time, was not recorded), because the raw-text push backstop reads the whole command, one segment at a time, before the 65,536-character size cap of the commit reading denies a longer one. Those shapes now include two that were measured separately, on 2026-10-18: a run of quoted '-c' mirror options with no blank, and a run of adjacent '<(' or '>(' process substitutions, each before a force-push to a protected branch. While the backstop read the first with the single mirror-configuration regex, whose cost grew with the square of the run's length, one call of this check on it took 14.0 s of CPU time at 256 KB and reached no decision within the 60-second hang guard of the hooks self-test at 1 MB; with the linear probe that replaced that regex, it took at most 0.47 s of CPU time at 1 MB. On the second, which the backstop's segment split now walks in place instead of copying the rest of the command for each substitution, it took about 0.17 s of CPU time at 1 MB. Each figure was measured in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4. Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

Registry-scoped: inert with no registry at the session cwd's git-resolved toplevel (no ancestor walk, unlike orch-truncation-guard; AIQT_ORCH_REQUIRE_REGISTRY is not read here), and an unreadable registry allows silently with no guard-events row. Blocks a blocking question ONLY when the declared operating-mode record reads as unattended (this guards one known mistake shape, a blocking prompt idling an unattended run; it is not a security boundary). The mode record fails CLOSED to that guards-armed (unattended) posture, so the question is denied, for every read of the mode path that ends in neither not found nor a decoded text, the deny naming the reason: a mode path holding a NUL character, or one that is not strict UTF-8 (a lone surrogate, which is also how a surrogate-escaped non-UTF-8 name arrives), refused fail-closed before any open even where the OS could open it; a file that cannot be opened or read (a permission error, a socket, whose non-blocking open itself fails (ENXIO on Linux), or a missing file under a parent path that is a regular file, whose open reports not a directory rather than not found); one that is not a regular file (a directory, a FIFO, or a device such as /dev/zero, refused by an fstat after the non-blocking open and before any read, so a FIFO with no writer does not wait); one larger than 1048576 bytes (the reader reads at most one byte more), or one whose bytes are not valid UTF-8; and, for the text read, in these cases: an Operating-mode: declaration whose value is empty or begins with neither attended nor unattended; or, with no declaration line, content that parses as JSON but is not exactly an object whose one key, mode, holds a string beginning with attended or unattended (a bare JSON scalar such as true, 42, null or a quoted string, an array, an object with other keys, or one whose mode is missing, not a string or unrecognized), or content beginning with {, [ or a double quote that does not parse as JSON (malformed, partial, trailing text, duplicate keys, or nesting too deep to parse). It fails OPEN, allowing the question, in these cases: no declared mode path, a file whose open reports not found, an empty or whitespace-only file, or content with no declaration line that does not parse as JSON and does not begin with {, [ or a double quote (prose, including prose beginning with a number or a word, such as 42 items done or true trailing); that fail-open is logged to guard-events (where that append fails, the call is still allowed, with a note saying the row could not be written). Every input ends in one of these answers or the attended allow below; only a stall the hook timeout bounds can delay it (a path lookup on a hung mount, a read from a stalled filesystem, or what a device driver's open does). An attended mode is allowed with no guard-events row. The deny instruction distinguishes record-and-continue for ordinary decisions from record-and-HOLD for anything at the human-oversight threshold; the hook redirects the question and never licenses acting without the answer. Each denied ask appends ONE idempotent machine row keyed on session_id plus tool_use_id, carrying a bounded redacted summary (question count, length, digest), never the question text, and a guard-events row; a failed guard-events append adds a short recording-failure warning to the deny reason and the banner while the deny stands. Its behaviour is verified by the behaviour self-test. It cannot see a blocking prompt raised outside the AskUserQuestion tool. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took under 0.01 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

A RECORDING substrate, not an enforcement point: it appends launch rows (a Bash call with run_in_background true, or a registry-declared dispatch tool) and completion rows (a TaskOutput read) to the machine-written dispatch ledger the stop guard consumes as its Gap-B oracle. It never blocks; a failed ledger write is surfaced as a non-blocking systemMessage, never swallowed, and a lease max_age_hours horizon that cannot be evaluated does not turn this recorder off: the row is recorded anyway and the cannot-evaluate is surfaced as a note (armed and surfaced, never a silent skip). Coverage is exactly the hooked tools: a launch through an unhooked tool is invisible (costing one spurious stop-guard deny), a completion that never passes through TaskOutput is invisible until the staleness horizon expires the row, and the task-id extraction from tool responses is best-effort field matching. Both blind-spot directions are bounded by staleness plus the resume audit, and disclosed at the stop guard.

gates.residue: Total over the surface it examines: an OPEN merge_pending row carrying a TYPED ref (pr:N, decision:X) whose merge or record evidence exists in the declared truth sources always fails the gate. It reads only typed structured refs; a narrative number in prose, an untyped row, or a register kept outside the declared surface is out of scope by design (D9), and drift the truth sources themselves cannot see (an unpushed local merge, a PR merged under a subject with no (#N) marker) passes. In a checkout with no orchestration registry the live leg is NOT APPLICABLE (the record is machine-local by design) and the self-test carries the assurance; that scope boundary is printed, never silent.

Partial over a best-effort, adopter-configured surface. It proves preservation only for column-zero H2 headings that the adopter's own regular expressions select and that are newly introduced on the branch (present at the branch tip, absent at the unique merge-base); it catches a clean section-drop but MISSES a section that was reworded, renamed, or moved (a changed heading reads as a new-and-dropped pair, not a preserved one), never compares section bodies, does not cover edits to a heading already present at merge-base, and cannot tell a valid supersession from an opt-out marker an author simply added. Any record path or heading outside the config, and any grammar the pattern does not match, is outside its surface. The config is trusted adopter input to this preservation check: rewriting it so its heading-pattern selects fewer or no headings (semantic narrowing that makes real sections stop matching) is a change to that trusted config, not a dropped section, and defending the config against adversarial narrowing is out of this gate's threat model (it is the config-integrity surface's concern). Missing or ambiguous inputs inside the declared surface (a duplicate selected heading, an unreadable declared record, an unresolvable ref, a config path whose final or any parent component is a symlink, a non-unique merge-base on EITHER the default or the explicit-base path, an explicit --base-ref that is not that unique merge-base, an explicit --branch-ref that disagrees with the observable second parent of a two-parent post-merge commit, a default config the merge itself deleted, an uninferable branch tip) fail closed (exit 2); an explicit --base-ref is accepted only when the merge-base is unique and the ref names it, so it cannot mask a drop by naming one of several merge-bases that disagree on a section, and when the post-merge commit has two parents an explicit --branch-ref must name the observable second parent, so it cannot mask a drop by comparing against the first parent. It also strips the ambient GIT_ environment before every git call so a redirected GIT_DIR or GIT_WORK_TREE cannot swap in a decoy repository, and it does not follow a symlinked config at the final or any parent component. Only with no adopter config present (a genuinely absent, not-a-symlink default) AND none at the pre-merge target is the gate NOT APPLICABLE by design; a config the merge removed, or one whose removal cannot be evaluated because the post-merge ref is unresolvable, fails closed instead. Pack CI exercises only the synthetic self-test while the adopter owns the live post-merge invocation.

It never exits 2 (a stop raised inside the core propagates, but an exit whose status would be 2 is re-raised as an exit with status 1), never blocks, never asks, and never alters orch-stop-guard's decision: a refresh only keeps a fresh lease fresh, it never re-arms a lapsed lease and never disarms a live one, so its order against the stop guard on the Stop event does not matter.

The barrier does not record that mode, so the two writers agree only when run with the same value; a doctor run without it can clear a barrier a registry-required SessionStart armed for a scope deny; clearing it does not allow any Bash call, because the barrier only warns and the guard denies on its own scope check. Arming and clearing are BEST-EFFORT and ATOMIC: both writers create a temporary file beside the barrier file, flush and fsync it, then rename it onto the barrier file with os.replace. Where the barrier cannot be written (its state directory cannot be created, the temporary file cannot be created or written, or the rename fails, for example XDG_STATE_HOME naming a regular file, or a full disk), the SessionStart audit removes the temporary file it created and ignores the error so SessionStart never wedges, the previous barrier file (armed or clear) or its absence is left byte-identical, the PreToolUse barrier therefore does not surface this run's findings, and the session still sees the SessionStart warning naming them (where opening the forced-exit log fails other than as not found, because the state directory cannot be searched or is not a directory, as with that regular file, the warning also names the forced-exit log as unreadable), and that warning then also says the barrier was not persisted (this audit did not arm it) and asks for a manual record instead of saying a re-run clears the barrier, naming the remedy (remove a directory at the barrier path, which neither audit can replace; otherwise make the state directory creatable and writable), while a clean audit that cannot clear the barrier adds no warning (a barrier it leaves armed still reads as armed, noted once per arming where its warned flag can be written, otherwise on each mutation outside the record surfaces, so one already warned about stays silent; a directory in its place reads as armed and is noted on each mutation outside the record surfaces); tools/orch_doctor.py --resume-audit does not ignore that error, its run ends with it, and the previous barrier file is left unchanged. The PreToolUse barrier reads the barrier file only where the registry loader reads the registry ok, and reads a barrier file that exists but is unreadable or malformed as armed (see orch-resume-barrier). Registry-scoped: silent where the registry loader reads the root's registry as absent; a root the loader cannot examine reads bad, not absent, and the audit warns. It reads records, git state, and the truncation guard's registry discovery only; it cannot detect a handoff that is stale in ways its declared grammar does not carry (free-text drift). Lease MISMATCH detection at this audit stays bounded to staleness, over the file mtime and, where the registry declares a lease heartbeat block, the declared heartbeat field too (an invalid declaration, an unevaluable heartbeat, and a stale or future heartbeat field are findings): these probes are shared with tools/orch_doctor.py --resume-audit, which runs with no session identity, so the holder field is not compared HERE; where the lease declares holder_is_session_id, each lease-scoped guard proves the payload session identity against the holder field per event, and the orch-lease-heartbeat controls surface a lost or taken lease to the session that last provably held it.

The mutation barrier behind orch-resume-audit, shipped WARN-FIRST (stage bake, a recorded posture): while the barrier state is armed it surfaces a systemMessage on the first mutation outside the allowlist (the record surfaces, the registry files, and the suite's own state directory stay writable, so the only exit, correcting the record, is never blocked), and it blocks nothing during the bake. The flip to deny is a manifest edit (stage to enforce, default to ask/deny) taken on recorded guard-events evidence after the bake period, per the guardrail-config-integrity discipline. Bash targets are not path-judged (a command's write targets are not lexically resolvable), so Bash mutations pass with the same surfacing only. Clearing the barrier requires re-running the audit (tools/orch_doctor.py --resume-audit) against corrected records; acknowledgement alone does not clear it. An absent barrier file (a dangling symlink included) reads as clear, and a symlink to a regular file reads as that file. The barrier is read with a non-blocking open (a FIFO with no writer does not wait for one), an fstat that refuses anything not a regular file before any read (so a FIFO or a device such as /dev/zero is never read), and a read bounded at 64 KiB. One that exists but is not a regular file (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory, or a symlink to any of these), is larger than the bound, cannot be read or parsed for any reason (including a RecursionError from deeply nested JSON), or is not a well-formed barrier (a JSON object whose keys are exactly a boolean active and a list of string findings, both required, plus an optional boolean warned and an optional string ts; a truncated write by an earlier writer is not), reads as ARMED, not absent: every mutation outside the allowlist then surfaces a note naming the file as unreadable or malformed with the reason (not once per arming, since there is no readable warned flag to record), which blocks nothing during the bake, and a mutation on the allowlist is allowed after the same read (a regular file on a filesystem that stalls, such as a hung network mount, can still stall the read until the hook timeout, as any file read can); it clears when the doctor's --resume-audit or the next SessionStart audit replaces the file (the rename replaces a FIFO, a device node or a symlink at the path and leaves a symlink's target intact), or when the user corrects or removes it (the state directory is on the allowlist), and where the state directory cannot be searched the replace fails too, so the note persists until its permissions are restored. Neither audit can replace a directory at the barrier path itself (the rename fails with IsADirectoryError), so for a directory the note says to remove the directory; a symlink to a directory gets the generic note, since the rename replaces the link. A writer removes the temporary file it created when any later step fails (writing, closing or renaming it) and never removes a temporary name it did not create; a process killed between creating and renaming it leaves that temporary file beside the barrier file. Recording the warned flag replaces the file atomically too; a failed replace leaves it unchanged, so the note surfaces again on the next mutation. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took under 0.01 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

PREVIEW CHANNEL ONLY: a standalone file installed by hand from .preview/, not part of the pack's plugin. After a CI rerun command that succeeds (gh run rerun, glab ci retry: a simple command, in a small closed shell grammar the hook reads exactly, whose words hold gh, run and rerun, or glab, ci and retry, in that order at any positions), or a recognized check command that failed and then passed with the same words, each as written with its quoting (pytest 'a  b' and pytest 'a b' differ; blanks and comments between words do not count), and no recorded change between, it adds a note after the tool call, and at turn end it refuses a final message that presents a pass as conclusive without naming the earlier failure, at most 2 times in a row, after which each later conclusive stop is allowed with a warning and the reruns stay outstanding. The refusal count is kept in the hook's state file, so the cap holds when the platform's stop_hook_active field is absent or true; the count is reset to 0 only by a UserPromptSubmit event, a Stop whose stop_hook_active field is explicitly false, or a final message that names a disclosure word, never by a tool call or an allowed stop, so without UserPromptSubmit registered and without that field, after 2 refusals each later conclusive stop is allowed with the warning until a disclosure (a missed refusal). An explicit false is trusted as a new turn, so a host that sends it on a Stop that continues a refusal is refused at every such Stop (the cap does not hold). A state file that is missing (the first use of a session cannot be told from a lost one), unreadable or malformed gives an unknown refusal count, never a fresh 0; while the state file cannot be read or is malformed, a conclusive turn end, or one with no final message, is allowed with a warning that the state could not be read, and once it is missing, or a tool call has written back a lost or unreadable one, until one of those reset signals a conclusive turn end is allowed with a warning in place of a refusal only while a rerun seen since is outstanding; any other is silent, and a lost record of earlier reruns is silent (a missed refusal); with neither UserPromptSubmit registered nor stop_hook_active explicitly false, every refusal is replaced by that warning until a disclosure (a missed refusal). It recognizes only the listed CI rerun and check commands run through the shell tool. A rerun through a web page, a pushed empty commit, a runner's own retry option, an API call such as gh api .../rerun, a gh alias, or a changed command line is not seen. The shell reading is exact only for the closed grammar described in the hook's docstring, which reads a command of at most 8192 characters. Inside the grammar, a CI rerun is missed only when its words come into existence when the command runs, or bash runs gh under another name: an expansion that has a value ($c run rerun, with c=gh), a tilde expansion (~ run rerun with HOME=/path/to/gh, ~+ run rerun with PWD=/path/to/gh, or ~-; bash tilde-expands a word the hook reads as a plain ~), a pathname expansion (/usr/bin/g? run rerun), an alias, a shell function, a hashed command name (hash -p /path/to/gh x; x run rerun), or a command string handed to another program (sh -c '...', eval '...', ssh, xargs input, a script). The name rule ignores command position, so a simple command that names gh, run and rerun in order without running them is noted anyway: echo gh run rerun, unquoted or with each word quoted alone (echo "gh" "run" "rerun"), command -v gh run rerun, a function body that is defined but never called, false && gh run rerun 7; true (a false note, and a false refusal when the call succeeds). The hook reads an exit status only from an integer exit-code field of the tool response, where one is present, and that status is the whole call's: a later command, || true, a background &, a ! or an if or while condition can hide a gh call the server refused (HTTP 403), with or without pipefail set, and so can a pipe under default bash options, so gh run rerun 7 2>&1 | tail -5, gh run rerun 7 || true, gh run rerun 7; echo done, gh run rerun 7 &, ! gh run rerun 7 and if gh run rerun 7; then :; fi exit 0 and are kept as certain (a false refusal); with pipefail set, the pipe form exits nonzero and gets the uncertain note only, and the other forms still exit 0. The note for a CI rerun call that succeeds says only that the call was not reported as failed and asserts neither a rerun nor an earlier failure, and the refusal asks the assistant to state any earlier failure; neither it nor the warning given when a refusal is capped or its count cannot be saved asserts a CI rerun (each says only that a command naming one was not reported as failed). Every command outside the grammar is a possible CI rerun by construction: the hook could not parse it, so a CI rerun cannot be ruled out, and no search of its text decides otherwise; this includes echo "$(date)", a here-document, a line continuation, ${x:-y}, $'...', a redirection spelling not listed, and any command longer than 8192 characters. Each nonblank one gets a note, even when it fails (a blank command gets no note), so an off-grammar command that reruns nothing (a here-document commit, notably) gets a false note. Such a command, and a CI rerun call that fails (the rerun may or may not have started), is an uncertain rerun: its note says that a CI rerun cannot be ruled out and asserts no rerun and no earlier check failure, and it is never kept, so it never brings a turn-end refusal; a real CI rerun written outside the grammar, a failed call that did start a rerun, and an off-grammar check command that fails and then passes each get their note and no refusal (a missed refusal). An off-grammar command also counts as a change unless it fails, so a local rerun across it gets no local-rerun note of its own, and a check command outside the grammar is never compared as a check. Read-only is decided only inside the grammar: env with any argument, an assignment prefix (X=1 ls), a command word holding an expansion, and any output redirection (> >> >| &> &>>) whose target is not the unquoted word /dev/null count as a change; an input redirection (< <<<) and a descriptor duplication or close (>&2, <&0, >&-) write nothing. Also: a failed call is never counted as a change, so a fix made by a command that then failed reads as no change (a false note); a change made outside the tool calls it sees reads as no change (a false note), and a read-only-looking command with a side effect reads as no change; a setup command that is not read-only beside a check (source venv/bin/activate && pytest, an export; cd, pushd, popd, set and tee are not counted) counts as a change, so a later rerun of that check alone is not flagged; pass and fail are read from the event name and a few response fields, not the output; the Stop check reads only the final message against fixed phrase lists, so a claim worded otherwise passes, a claim after an unlisted negation is refused, any disclosure word clears the reruns wherever it stands, even inside a denial such as I did not rerun CI, whether or not the failure is recorded; it does not record or investigate the failure itself; with a state file that cannot be read or is malformed, a final message that presents a pass as conclusive without a disclosure word, or a payload with no final message, is allowed with a warning that the state could not be read, and any other final message is allowed silently; while reruns are outstanding, a payload with no final message is allowed with a warning that says so; with no state location at all (no session key in the payload, or no absolute state directory) nothing is kept and every stop is allowed silently; a refusal whose count cannot be saved is allowed with a warning, also on a Stop whose stop_hook_active field is explicitly false; concurrent hook runs are serialized by a lock file beside the state file, and a run saves only while that lock file and the state file are the ones it locked and loaded: a run that cannot take the lock within 2 seconds saves nothing (a tool call's change or rerun is not recorded, a prompt does not reset the count) and allows a turn end it would refuse with a warning that names the lock, and a run whose lock file is deleted or replaced while it holds it (also one moved away and put back after another run saved), or whose state file another run saved meanwhile, saves nothing and allows a turn end it would refuse with a warning that the refusal count cannot be saved (a deletion, replacement or save that lands in the few system calls between its last check and its write can still let one stale save through, and so can a save whose state file matches the loaded one in device, inode, size, modification time and change time, all five fields it compares, as when an inode number is reused within the filesystem's timestamp granularity); while the lock cannot be taken at all (a lock path that is a symbolic link or not a regular file, a lock file it cannot open, a filesystem that refuses flock, a platform without flock), it keeps no state, so it only notes after each tool call and, with no state saved before then, every turn end passes silently (a missed refusal), while the outstanding reruns of a state saved before then still bring a warning; a state folder moved away or deleted during a session is read as no state, so the next turn end passes silently (a missed refusal); nothing removes its state and lock files, one of each per session; a state file written by an earlier revision of the hook (without the current state version) is discarded and read as no earlier runs, so none of its flags arms a refusal and a local rerun across it is missed; a state file of the current version holding a flag of a kind this version never keeps is malformed, but the state file is trusted: a hand-edited state of the current version whose flags carry a prefix this version keeps still arms a refusal; a check run again with a word quoted another way ('a b', then "a b") is a different check (a missed note), and so is one with an operator spelled another way (pytest -q; ls, then pytest -q && ls, or a newline in place of the ;), while leading and trailing newlines and a final ; do not count; a check command whose words hold an expansion (a $ expansion, or an unquoted * ? or ~) is never compared with another run, so its fail-then-pass gets no local-rerun note (a missed note, never a false one); a command holding a tab, a newline or another control character (C0, DEL or C1) is shown in a note as one $'...' string with those characters escaped; and the hook fails open on its own failure (warn-only by design: an advisory hook must not block on its own failure): an internal error exits 0 with no output, an unreadable state file is read as no earlier runs (so a local rerun across it is missed) with an unknown refusal count (a Stop that reads it allows a conclusive stop with a warning that the state could not be read), though the current call's own CI rerun or possible CI rerun note is still given, and a note or refusal that cannot be written to stdout is dropped.

gates.residue: Total over the declared register: a broken digest chain or sequence, a reused id, an illegal status transition, a rewrite of anchored or merge-base rows, and an unverifiable landed row always fail; a declared-but-unreadable register, a malformed or unreadable anchor, an anchor entry that exists but is not a usable regular file (a dangling symlink or a directory; presence is an explicit lstat whose only absence answer is ENOENT, so such an entry, or an anchor lstat failure such as EIO, never takes the missing-anchor allowance), a present registry that is not a JSON object, a git failure, launch error or timeout deciding whether the register is tracked or reading its merge-base authority, and a launch error or timeout reading whether a landed row's commit exists, are exit 2. The anchor write (--update-anchor, tracked and untracked registers alike) never opens an existing entry: a non-regular anchor entry (a symlink, dangling or live, included) is refused with its target neither created nor rewritten, and a green advance lands by atomic replace of an exclusively created temporary. A same-authority local file offers no protection against an actor who rewrites the WHOLE chain and the anchor together, which defeats the untracked mode (the tracked mode is bounded by merge-base history instead), so rewrites are DETECTABLE within those bounds, never prevented; adopters needing real separation bind the same interface to a server-side append store. The landed-row check proves the cited commit and check path exist, not that the check semantically guards the mistake. In a checkout with no registry the live leg is NOT APPLICABLE with the self-test as assurance.

inside a steps: block (a plain bare steps: key; one with a same-line value is cannot-evaluate) the first entry must be a '- ' item and every line at the item or step-key indentation must be a plain unquoted identifier key from the closed step-key set (name, run, uses, with, env, if, id, shell, working-directory, continue-on-error, timeout-minutes), a plain key outside that set or a line the step model cannot place being cannot-evaluate, a LITERAL block's content bounded by the KEY column so a sibling step key after a dashed '- run: |' block re-enters those rules instead of being consumed as block content, and every shell: value READ under a closed classification (a bare known non-python shell keyword, bash, sh, pwsh, powershell or cmd, is clean; every other shell: value, an isolation-claiming python template included, is cannot-evaluate), while deeper with:/env: input VALUES keep the line-form handling (a shell:-spelled input KEY is read as a shell template, a disclosed over-read) and a plain key other than run: and shell: outside a steps: block remains unscanned (the step tracker is single-level); an empty run: value, a bare run: or one whose only same-line text is a YAML comment (YAML strips it to the same empty value), is read ONLY in the two proven shapes, a next-line plain scalar or a next-line block header whose content is deeper than both the header and the key, and is null only when the next non-blank, non-comment line is not deeper than the key; a comment line before a deeper value, a header with no content deeper than the key (a header at the end of the text included) or with content at or above its own column, a line opening with '#' directly after that header (YAML block content the reader refuses rather than reads), any other run: value starting with | or > on the key line or that deeper line, a node property or alias, or a plain scalar continued onto a further deeper line is cannot-evaluate, exit 2, never skipped, each naming the file and line), and the PATH provenance of python3 itself; a python3 token embedded in a quoted argument or a heredoc may be miscounted.

a verify= or verify_ssl= that is not a true-valued literal (False, 0, None and an empty string are false-valued), an ssl= that is False or 0, a .verify attribute set to anything but a true-valued literal, any reference to _create_unverified_context, _create_stdlib_context, _create_default_https_context, CERT_NONE, CERT_OPTIONAL or CLIENT_AUTH, an ssl.SSLContext whose protocol is not proven ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT, and a check_hostname or verify_mode (cert_reqs=) set, by assignment, any other store (an unpacked, for, with or comprehension target), literal setattr or keyword, to anything but True or a proven ssl.CERT_REQUIRED, and a standard-library client whose default context skips certificate checks (smtplib.SMTP_SSL, poplib.POP3_SSL and ftplib.FTP_TLS whose context=, imaplib.IMAP4_SSL whose ssl_context=, and any method named starttls or stls, called as x.starttls(...) or getattr(x, 'starttls')(...), whose context (called on an imported or locally defined class, as in smtplib.SMTP.starttls(server), the first positional argument is self) is not proven a verifying context: a call of ssl.create_default_context() (no purpose, or a proven ssl.Purpose.SERVER_AUTH) or ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT) with no * or unreadable ** spread, or a name every binding of which, in every scope Python may read it from, is such a call; so an absent or None context, a parameter (a None default included), an attribute (self.context), a name with any other binding (a walrus, a starred unpacking, a conditional rebinding, a copy of another name, an import) and any other expression are findings (a bare annotation such as ctx: object, or a del, is no binding); any ssl.get_server_certificate, which never checks the hostname whatever ca_certs it is given; a logging.handlers.SMTPHandler whose secure= is set or hidden by a spread), each also when referenced without a call, and a server_hostname= that is an empty literal (seccry); a subprocess run/call/check_call/check_output/Popen whose shell is on, or unseen through a non-literal ** spread, a * spread or a ninth positional argument, over a non-literal command, and os.system, os.popen, posix.system, nt.system, subprocess.getoutput/getstatusoutput, asyncio.create_subprocess_shell (asyncio.subprocess included) and loop.subprocess_shell over a non-literal command or one a spread hides (secinp); and any reference to eval or exec (builtins included), types.FunctionType and the runpy, timeit, cProfile, profile, pdb and code runners, and any call of or reference to a method named exec_module or load_module, whatever object it is called on (secinp); a method judged by its name alone (starttls, stls, subprocess_shell, exec_module, load_module) referenced without a call, as x.name or getattr(x, 'name'), is an alias and a finding. Names resolve per scope as Python binds them, so a binding in another function never hides the one in force, and every binding a module, class or comprehension scope may hold is a candidate; an unbound name falls back to the builtin of that name where one exists. A sink module reached as an attribute of another module names that module (shutil.os.system is os.system; from logging.handlers import pickle binds pickle), except an attribute named like the module holding it (timeit.timeit). getattr(x, 'name') is read as x.name, and so is a name or attribute directly followed by a string literal in a call's positional arguments or a tuple or list display (the monkeypatch idiom (os, 'system') reads os.system), except in setattr, delattr, hasattr and a mock patch.object, which store, delete or test the attribute. A sink module (every dotted prefix of every named sink, derived from the sink sets, so multiprocessing.reduction, logging.handlers and torch are included) used other than as an attribute base (m.x; the first argument of getattr, setattr, delattr or a mock patch.object with a literal name; the argument of hasattr; or the name so read with a string literal) is a finding: bound to another name in any form (assignment, unpacking, walrus, conditional or boolean expression, default parameter, match capture, for or with target), passed as an argument, returned, yielded, held in a container, or passed to getattr with a non-literal name, unless a string literal directly follows it (out of scope, below). A judged callable referenced without a call, a literal dynamic import of a sink module, and a star import from a named sink module are also findings. Keywords are read as Python binds them: a literal ** dict by its keys, and so a ** or dict(...) inside it at any depth, in overwrite order (a duplicate key keeping its last value; a non-literal spread inside it leaves the keys written before it unseen, though a literal verify, ssl, check_hostname, server_hostname, verify_mode, cert_reqs or allow_pickle written there is still judged), and dict(...) only where dict can only be the builtin. A safe value (a yaml Loader, an SSLContext protocol, a verify_mode or cert_reqs, a client's context) is proven only when every binding the name may hold names it (for a context, is a call of a verifying constructor); a name that may also hold an assignment, a parameter or any other value the lint cannot name, an unbound name, and an expression prove nothing, so they are findings. A current legitimate site is admitted only by a reviewed in-gate allowlist entry (path, enclosing qualname, kind, exact count, reason line), and a count that no longer matches is itself a finding; the shipped entries are self-test mutant, fixture, stub, fault-injection, deny-table, static-analysis and own-source loader sites over the repository's own source. Each file is decoded as Python decodes it (a BOM and a PEP 263 coding cookie honoured); a cookie other than utf-8, a file it cannot stat, read, decode or parse, a directory it cannot list or search (each plugin directory and its hooks directory included), any symlink inside a scanned root or directly under plugin/, a missing root and a non-regular *.py entry are cannot-evaluate (exit 2), never a clean pass. Per rule, NOT covered: for secdsz, deserialization in other languages and file formats, deserializers outside the named set, and dispatch the lint cannot see; for seccry, the choice of algorithm, mode, key size and other parameters, weak, deprecated or home-grown schemes, and protection of data at rest (only certificate and hostname verification in transit is linted); for secinp, validation of external input for type, range and format at the boundary, and the SQL, markup and template injection classes (only the operating-system command and code-execution sinks are linted, by literalness). Out of scope: this lint guards against ACCIDENTAL use of a dangerous API in the repository's own code written the ordinary way, so code deliberately built to hide a sink is not claimed: a string-assembled or string-literal module name (importlib or __import__ with a computed name, sys.modules[...]; a literal import of a sink module is a finding, but the module it returns is not followed), getattr with a computed name or a sink module followed by an adjacent string literal (f(os, 'x') and (pickle, 'x')[0] read the module as an attribute base, not an escape, and getattr(shutil, 'os') is not read as the os module), __builtins__ aliasing (m = __builtins__, __builtins__.exec, __builtins__[...]), a rewritten module attribute (ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT = 2 still proves the protocol) and dunder access (__getattribute__, __setattr__, object.__setattr__, __dict__). It also does NOT catch: dynamic dispatch (getattr with a non-literal name on an object other than a sink module, setattr with a non-literal name, globals() or vars() lookups); a numpy.load reached through an alias and given allow_pickle positionally; an attribute chain whose base is not an import binding (a parameter, self, a call result or a subscript, so self.os.system and sys.modules['os'].system are not resolved); a sink module re-exported under a name other than its own (mod._p.loads where mod binds pickle as _p); a sink function obtained from such an object or from a call; a method run on a profiler, debugger or trace object; a shell reached through an argv list that names a shell (sh -c) or a Python interpreter given code (sys.executable with -c or -m), an executable= override, or os.exec*, os.spawn* or pty.spawn of a shell; a verify, verify_ssl, ssl, check_hostname, server_hostname, verify_mode, cert_reqs or allow_pickle value hidden in, or overwritten by, a non-literal ** spread (a literal ** dict is read by its keys at any depth, in Python's overwrite order; only the subprocess shell switch and the command, Loader, protocol, context and secure= of the judged sinks are denied when unseen), and a verify given positionally (Session.merge_environment_settings(url, proxies, stream, verify, cert)); a verifying context changed after it is built other than by a check_hostname or verify_mode store (its trust store replaced through load_verify_locations, or a setattr with a computed name), and a context= given to a client whose default verifies (urllib, http.client, asyncio ssl=), judged only where the context is built; a starttls or stls called on a class reached other than through an import binding or a locally defined class (read as bound) and a client configured from logging.config data; TLS verification disabled inside a third-party library's defaults, through a library option it does not name, or through environment variables; a sink whose literal arguments are still attacker-shaped (the lint judges literalness, not data flow); and code outside the scanned roots (the vendored tree, .github, .preview, site, and Python embedded in a non-.py file). The allowlist reasons are maintainer-reviewed assertions; the gate checks their presence and count, not their truth, so a reviewed site replaced by an unsafe one in the same function at the same count passes. Its linkage to secenc (output encoded for its sink) and secout (generated output is untrusted input) is arguable, so none is claimed.
