a verify, verify_ssl, ssl, check_hostname, server_hostname, verify_mode, cert_reqs or allow_pickle value hidden in, or overwritten by, a non-literal ** spread (a literal ** dict is read by its keys at any depth, in Python's overwrite order; only the subprocess shell switch and the command, Loader, protocol, context and secure= of the judged sinks are denied when unseen), and a verify given positionally (Session.merge_environment_settings(url, proxies, stream, verify, cert)); a verifying context changed after it is built other than by a check_hostname or verify_mode store (its trust store replaced through load_verify_locations, or a setattr with a computed name), and a context= given to a client whose default verifies (urllib, http.client, asyncio ssl=), judged only where the context is built; a starttls or stls called on a class reached other than through an import binding or a locally defined class (read as bound) and a client configured from logging.config data; TLS verification disabled inside a third-party library's defaults, through a library option it does not name, or through environment variables; a sink whose literal arguments are still attacker-shaped (the lint judges literalness, not data flow); and code outside the scanned roots (the vendored tree, .github, .preview, site, and Python embedded in a non-.py file). The allowlist reasons are maintainer-reviewed assertions; the gate checks their presence and count, not their truth, so a reviewed site replaced by an unsafe one in the same function at the same count passes. Its linkage to secenc (output encoded for its sink) and secout (generated output is untrusted input) is arguable, so none is claimed.

A pattern scanner for hardcoded credentials: it catches recognizable provider-token prefixes (now including Google, Stripe, GitLab, SendGrid, npm, PyPI upload, and Slack webhook shapes), assignments of a literal to a credential-named variable, and high-entropy literals of 40 or more characters assigned to a generic credential-like name (Shannon entropy at least 3.5 bits per character judged on the token's first 150 characters, letters and digits required, placeholders and environment lookups excluded, metadata-named variables excluded). It still misses a keyword-free high-entropy string (the opaque-name class, R1, the measured residue of 2026-08-08 shared with gitleaks), a generic-keyword value of 12 to 39 characters that gitleaks can flag below the local 40-character floor (R3, a deliberate noise-control choice, confirmed against pinned gitleaks 8.30.1), a real secret held under a metadata-named variable such as public_key or key_path (excluded by design in the safe direction, where CI still catches it, R4); a deferred provider family (a Twilio-class short-prefix-over-hex or a Telegram bot token, left to gitleaks, R2); a secret split across lines or assembled by concatenation, an encoded secret, or a secret in a binary (R5); and an unquoted value that begins with an environment-lookup root such as process.env., treated as a reference not a literal (R6). What it reads: a file is scanned only when its name is a dotenv name (.env, or starting .env., in any case), its suffix is on the curated text allow-list, or it has no suffix, and only outside the .git, node_modules, __pycache__ and .working directories and other than the scanner source itself; any other file (an image, a binary key store, a text format off the allow-list) is never read. A dotenv or allow-listed file that is not valid UTF-8 is still scanned, decoded losslessly with each undecodable byte kept as a placeholder that is neither a word character nor a line break, so an ASCII secret beside a single stray byte is still caught; two or more stray non-ASCII bytes that together form a valid UTF-8 letter decode as that letter, so beside a token they break its word boundary and can hide it (the same word-boundary behaviour as in valid UTF-8 text). A scanned file that starts with a UTF-32 byte-order mark is ALSO scanned through a UTF-32 wide view beside the lossless byte view (the decode keeps an unpaired surrogate via surrogatepass; a scalar above U+10FFFF or a truncated final unit falls back to a replace decode whose U+FFFD placeholders are neither word characters nor line breaks, so a token before or after a four-byte-aligned bad unit is still matched), and a file that starts with a UTF-16 byte-order mark and has even length is ALSO scanned as UTF-16 (surrogatepass; a file whose first four bytes form the little-endian UTF-32 mark, which begins with the UTF-16-LE mark, keeps the UTF-16 reading as a further view beside the UTF-32 and byte views when its UTF-32 surrogatepass decode fails and its length is even), the views merged, so a byte-order-mark-prefixed file that actually holds 8-bit or ASCII text (almost any even-length byte string decodes as UTF-16, so a successful decode alone proves little) keeps the lossless-view coverage it had before the wide views. The merge drops duplicates per reported line and label, never per secret: two DIFFERENT tokens that share a path, view-relative line number and label (one per view) are reported as ONE finding, so the FAIL total counts reported findings, not an inventory of distinct credentials. UTF-16 or UTF-32 without a byte-order mark and other non-UTF-8 encodings are not decoded as such, so a secret in them can be missed; a byte-order mark in the middle of a file selects no wide view; mixed-width content behind one leading mark is decoded at that mark width only (the overlapping little-endian UTF-32/UTF-16 mark case is the one kept mixed reading); a declared-text odd-length UTF-16-marked file keeps only the lossless byte view, where the NULs of a real UTF-16 secret defeat the patterns; an odd-length file that begins with the overlapping little-endian UTF-32 mark keeps no UTF-16 reading at all (its wide view is the UTF-32 replace decode), so a UTF-16 secret in it can be missed, and a suffixless one of that shape is still decoded and scanned rather than named on a SKIP line; and stray bytes in the middle of a UTF-32 file misalign every later unit, so only a truncated final unit is recovered. Otherwise only a suffixless file that is not valid UTF-8 and took no wide view (no UTF-32 mark; a UTF-16 mark with odd length) is treated as binary and skipped, named on a SKIP line, so an extensionless key file carrying one stray byte and no byte-order mark is skipped too. Detection here is a compensating control, never a substitute for keeping the secret out of the repository in the first place.

hooks.residue: A COMPENSATING control, not a replacement: the CI secret-scan and gitleaks gates remain the broader backstop, and this layer moves the same high-signal detection to the moment a secret would be written, so an accidental paste is caught before it lands on disk rather than only at commit or CI time. It SINGLE-SOURCES its shapes from tools/check_secrets.py (the pack source of truth), rendered into the handler by tools/gen_secret_patterns.py and drift-gated so the two can never fork: the recognizable provider-token PREFIX shapes (GitHub, GitHub fine-grained PAT, OpenAI-style, OpenAI project key, Anthropic, AWS access key id, Slack, Slack app-level token, a private key block header, a JWT, and (GD-121) Google API key, Stripe live and test, GitLab personal access token, SendGrid, npm, PyPI upload token, and a Slack incoming-webhook URL), the credential-named ASSIGN shape (a passwd/password/secret/token/api-key/access-key/client-secret/auth-token/private-key/credential variable assigned a literal of real length), and (GD-121) an ENTROPY-GATED generic-assignment shape: a token of 40 or more characters (Shannon entropy at least 3.5 bits per character judged on its first 150 characters, letters and digits required) assigned to a generic credential-like name matched on EXACT components (key/auth/token/secret/passphrase/creds/... so apiKey and client-secret match while monkey and author do not), with placeholders and environment lookups excluded before the entropy test and a metadata-named left-hand side (id/name/version/url/path/public/...) excluded. It EXCLUDES obvious placeholders (the shared PLACEHOLDER shape: your/my/the-prefixed names, change-me, example, sample, dummy, redacted, fake, test, todo, none, null, n/a, an angle-bracket or dollar-brace or dollar-VAR template, and runs of x/dot/star), and for an UNQUOTED assignment value it additionally requires both a letter and a digit, exactly as check_secrets.py does, so ordinary prose does not trip it. It scans the content a Write would write, the new_string an Edit would introduce, the concatenation of the new_string values a MultiEdit would introduce across its edits, or the command string a Bash call would emit, and DENIES on a real match, naming only the pattern label and never echoing the secret value. DISCLOSED non-catches: a KEYWORD-FREE high-entropy value (an opaque = <hex> with no credential keyword near it): both this scanner and gitleaks miss it (R1, the measured residue of 2026-08-08); a generic-keyword value of 12 to 39 characters, below the local 40-character floor, which gitleaks can still flag (R3, a deliberate noise-control choice confirmed against pinned gitleaks 8.30.1); a real secret held under a metadata-named variable such as public_key or key_path, excluded here in the safe direction where the CI scan still catches it (R4); a secret written by a tool other than Write, Edit, MultiEdit, or Bash (other content tools such as NotebookEdit are out of scope, routed to a periodic pattern review); a secret split across tokens or lines or assembled by concatenation, since the scan is per-line and lexical; on the Bash path the command string is scanned as RAW TEXT (it is not shlex-tokenized and is not executed), so a secret assembled by concatenation or supplied through a shell variable or expansion is missed, but a redirect or an embedded # does NOT cause a Bash-path miss; the ASSIGN shape also does not match a JSON-style quoted credential key ("api_key": "...") or a triple-quoted value, a curated-pattern-set format-completeness gap routed to the periodic pattern review (backlog L12); a deferred provider family (a Twilio-class short-prefix-over-hex or a Telegram bot token, left to gitleaks, R2); an unquoted value beginning with an environment-lookup root such as process.env., treated as a reference not a literal (R6); and a base64-encoded or otherwise obfuscated form. gitleaks in CI is a BROADER independent scanner and a stronger net, but it is NOT exhaustive (it too misses the keyword-free entropy class R1), so it is a compensating layer, never a guarantee. It is BEST-EFFORT: it targets the accidental paste or commit, not an adversary deliberately encoding or fragmenting a secret to evade it. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 0.29 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

A BEST-EFFORT QUOTE-AWARE LEXICAL check via the shared tokenizer (_lex_command); it is DENY-and-educate (NO-ASK posture: this guard never returns an ask; read every ASK/ASKS/over-ASK below as that DENY-and-educate outcome, which NAMES the safe rewrite), so a detected substitution is denied with the reachable correct action rather than silently allowed, and it makes NO soundness or universal-coverage claim. In a parsed simple segment it resolves the effective command word past leading shell assignments and the recognized command modifiers command, exec, builtin, nohup, time, !, and env; for env it skips leading option tokens, the separated operands of common value-taking options, and NAME=VALUE assignments. When that word is literal git and the subcommand after recognized Git-global options is literal commit, it scans EVERY argv token after commit, including tokens after `--` or `--end-of-options`, for a backtick or $( marker in a substituting double-quoted or unquoted context, using the shared lexer's parallel per-token opacity plus the narrow unquoted-$( split form where a final opaque token ending in $ is immediately followed by the ( operator. It deliberately does no Git option binding because the shell expands argv before Git parses it. On an unparseable command, the raw fallback ASKS when coarse git-commit and substitution-marker probes both match; that fallback can over-match quoted prose or literal markers. HONEST RESIDUALS: the option tokens belonging to a recognized command modifier are not skipped (for example command -p git commit, time -p git commit, exec -c git commit, exec -a x git commit, and nohup -- git commit), so resolution advances one word past the modifier, stops on the option, and silently ALLOWs a substitution-bearing commit; command modifiers outside the recognized set (notably sudo, nice, timeout, doas, stdbuf, and ionice) are not resolved, so for example sudo git commit -m "$(x)" silently ALLOWs; reserved-word compounds (if/while/until and `{ ...; }`) are not parsed through to their inner git command; shell functions and aliases that rename git; git-config subcommand aliases (for example alias.ci=commit making git ci -m "$(x)") cannot be known lexically and silently ALLOW; sh -c or bash -c script bodies; eval or xargs indirection; redirect targets on a recognized commit segment are removed from argv by the lexer and are not scanned, so git commit -m ok > "$(x)" and git commit -m ok 2> "`x`" silently ALLOW; leading environment-assignment values and Git-global option/value tokens before commit; a pre-subcommand unquoted $( that fragments the lexer segment, letting the whole commit invocation including its message escape inspection; quote-mangled command words such as g''it are outside the claimed command-resolution surface even where the shared lexer happens to normalize a form to git; $VAR indirection, concatenation, PATH-shadowed commands, and any other non-literal command word that does not resolve lexically to git; commands outside the Bash tool; and unparseable commands beyond the raw fallback probes. Deliberate over-ASKs: $((...)) includes $(; a bare $ immediately before an escaped parenthesis (for example git commit -m $\(x\)) is marked opaque and the decoded-marker check sees $(, so it ASKS even though Bash passes literal $(x) and runs no substitution; ANSI-C $'...' is treated as an opaque marker-bearing token even though Bash does not substitute inside it; whole-token opacity means an escaped literal backtick or $( sharing a word with an unrelated unquoted expansion or glob prompts; and a post-boundary pathspec produced by substitution (for example git commit -- $(ls)) prompts because the shell still executes it. It targets the accidental case, not an adversary. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 0.24 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

A PATH guard, not a content judge: it decides where a write lands, never what it writes. Covers only PreToolUse Write, Edit, and MultiEdit calls carrying a readable file_path. TWO arming inputs, each fail-open on genuine ABSENCE only: the per-slice declaration write-scope.json, read at the orchestration registry-declared state_dir (resolved from the registry the guard reads EXACTLY ONCE, via the pure _state_dir_from_registry helper, never a second independently-faulting read; out of the slice tree by default but MAY be in-tree when the registry declares an in-tree state_dir), arms SLICE CONFINEMENT; the in-tree committed frozen floor .aiqt/frozen.json (generated by tools/gen_manifest.py from the ownership classification, drift-gated) arms the FROZEN layer. The structural other-repo/nested-repo denial applies to every covered write whose repository root resolves; the frozen-floor denial fires whenever a floor is PRESENT, and an armed session additionally requires one, so neither is unconditionally always-on and only an un-armed session with a genuinely-absent floor leaves the frozen layer inert. Slice confinement is fail-open on a missing declaration. The principled fail-open is genuine ABSENCE (of a declaration or floor: no confinement in effect, the same inert boundary gensrc and, by default, the orchestration suite use, whose truncation guard denies an absent registry in the opt-in registry-required mode); a cannot-evaluate FAULT is not absence and denies (see the fail posture below). The registry that LOCATES the declaration is part of the read: a bad or unreadable registry (an lstat fault, a read/parse error, a non-version-1 object, or a present-but-malformed state_dir) is a cannot-evaluate that DENIES rather than silently falling back to XDG and disarming confinement. Out-of-scope is a DENY, never an ASK (an ASK would hand the confined actor the click-through on its own confinement and would wedge an unattended run); the remedy is the harness re-declaring the slice, so scope-widening stays on the harness side, never a guarded-tool call. The declaration is machine-set inert data, never authored by the assistant through a guarded tool; the residual Bash-write path to the state dir remains, so the harness-set integrity is defence in depth, not categorical. Fail posture, by regime: a MISSING tool_name denies (the shared fail-closed contract); a malformed tool_name, an unreadable tool_input, a missing/empty file_path, or a control-character file_path denies as a malformed call in either regime; a covered write whose session repository root cannot be resolved (a missing/unreadable cwd or a non-git session) DENIES fail-closed in both regimes, because the root is resolved FIRST and containment cannot be evaluated without it, so this denial precedes any relative-path handling (a non-git relative-path write DENIES, it does not defer); only WHEN the root resolves does an un-armed relative file_path defer to the sibling absolute_paths hook (which owns the relative case, EN-8 making no cwd-trusting determination) and allow, while an armed relative file_path denies; an un-armed realpath/containment/nested-repo-probe FAULT now DENIES too (a cannot-evaluate: the guard cannot prove the target is in-repo and not nested, so it denies rather than allowing an unverified write), as the same fault does armed; a target proven OUTSIDE the session toplevel, or in a NESTED or FOREIGN git repository under or beside it (resolved via the scrubbed git toplevel of the target nearest existing ancestor, every ambient GIT_* removed so a decoy repo cannot redirect the read), denies in BOTH regimes UNLESS the target repo is an adopter-DECLARED COMPANION STORE (the sanctioned cross-repo path below); a present frozen floor with the target on it denies in both regimes (the floor outranks the allowlist, deny over allow), a present-but-malformed floor denies (cannot-evaluate), and an ABSENT floor is inert un-armed but denies while armed (an armed session must commit a floor, an explicit empty list being valid, so a Bash-deleted floor cannot silently downgrade an armed session); armed, a declaration that is unreadable, malformed, unknown-version, or whose worktree_root does not resolve to this repo (a stale, copied, or moved declaration) denies; an allow entry wholly on the frozen floor makes the declaration malformed and denies (a declaration cannot declare past the floor); a target in repo, not frozen, and in the declared slice scope allows silently, while one not in scope denies. Every deny appends a guard-events row (the over-fire metric) where the root is resolvable (with no resolvable root no row is attempted); a failed append leaves no row and adds a short recording-failure warning to the deny reason and the banner, never blocking or altering the denial. Matching is on canonicalized real paths with component-boundary tree containment (the gensrc idiom), never a raw string prefix; the declaration and floor share one entry grammar (a repo-root-relative POSIX path, a trailing / marks a tree, no absolute/backslash/./../control-char/wildcard component). The floor is enforced against the manifest CLASS set {derived, manifest-self, archive}. The RUNTIME value of that floor is un-lowerable by the constrained actor through the guarded tools (a guarded write to .aiqt/frozen.json is itself on the floor and denied); but its DEFINITION (FROZEN_CLASSES in tools/gen_manifest.py) is generator source that lands through pull-request review PLUS the drift gate, which detects an INCONSISTENT floor (a committed frozen.json that does not match a fresh regeneration), NOT an unauthorized-but-internally-consistent redefinition of the class set followed by regeneration; an independent floor-authorization mechanism is out of scope for this hook. The floor proves membership in its declared selector set only, not that the generation-time class mapping is semantically complete. Class c (partial), matching the sibling gensrc_guard: the control fires deterministically inside its Write|Edit|MultiEdit matcher, but the rules it enforces span write paths the matcher cannot see (Bash-mediated writes, NotebookEdit, filesystem MCP tools, any write outside the platform hook path), and its slice-arming state is machine-local, so CI cannot observe the confinement. The committed frozen floor .aiqt/frozen.json is a generated, drift-gated output backstopped at merge by the manifest-gen-drift gate (tools/gen_manifest.py --check), the gensrc-registry-drift gate (tools/gen_gensrc.py --check), and the independent manifest-integrity verifier (tools/check_manifest.py) (defence in depth, each catching the other residual; these CI gates are not removed or softened), but nothing backstops an uncommitted, out-of-scope-mutable, or cross-repository write through the uncovered channels. Realpath closes symlink escapes present at check time but not a post-check swap, hard-link alias, bind-mount change, or case-fold/Unicode alias between the lstat probe and the tool write (TOCTOU); an OS-level write sandbox is the stronger overlapping control where available. It is single-author by design: exactly one declaration, one writer, harness-replaced; it is confinement of the sole writer, not parallel-write collision arbitration. SANCTIONED COMPANION-STORE declaration (adopter-controlled config): the orchestration registry MAY declare companion_stores, a list of ABSOLUTE paths to git repo TOPLEVELS beside the session repo (for example the durable store the sole orchestrator owns, which is by design a SECOND git repo next to the code repo). A covered write whose target resolves - by EXACT repo-root match, the resolved git toplevel of the target EQUALLING a declared store root, never a prefix/substring - into a DECLARED companion store is ALLOWED and AUDITED (a guard-event row, kind wrtscp, decision allow, naming the declared store; where that append fails the write is still allowed, with a note saying the row could not be written) rather than denied, so the single most routine legitimate cross-repo write no longer inverts to deny-the-audited-path while the Bash residual stays open. The hook only HONOURS a validly-declared store, it never self-widens: per guard-input-soundness a declaration is honoured only if it is a non-empty absolute string resolving to a REAL git toplevel that IS the declared root itself; a MALFORMED, unresolvable, non-repo, or non-root declaration is fail-closed (silently dropped, the cross-repo write still DENIES), a bad entry can only remove a would-be allow and never open a hole, and the exact-root match means a write into a repo NESTED inside a declared store, or a sibling merely beside it, does NOT match. Declaring a store never defeats the frozen-floor or the nested-in-session denials. Declaring a companion store is a GUARDRAIL-CONFIGURATION change: companion_stores widens where covered writes may land (a cross-repo scope widening), so it is under the SAME human-authorization discipline as any other scope widening (guardrail-config-integrity) - the harness/adopter sets it, never the constrained actor. For that reason the orchestration LOCAL registry (.aiqt/orchestration.local.json) is on the hook-side ALWAYS-FROZEN set: a covered Write/Edit/MultiEdit to it is DENIED in BOTH regimes and INDEPENDENT of the committed frozen floor, so the actor cannot self-declare a companion_stores widening through a guarded tool (the general Bash-write path stays the disclosed residual). The companion_stores declaration is honoured only inside a VERSION-1 registry OBJECT: a registry with a missing or non-1 version reads as bad (a cannot-evaluate), so a declaration lacking "version": 1 yields NO stores and the cross-repo write FAILS CLOSED (denies), never silently taking effect. The declaration lives in the adopter/harness registry surface (exactly as state_dir does); this path guard reads it, it does not police who wrote the registry. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 0.04 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

SessionStart cannot block at the platform (exit 2 shows stderr only, doc-confirmed 2026-08-29), so this layer SURFACES divergence and ARMS the PreToolUse resume barrier; the barrier is the mechanism. Probes, all fail-closed to a finding rather than a silent pass: the declared handoff's Branch line against the real HEAD (scrubbed read-only probe), a handoff gate marker's commit against the real HEAD commit, lease staleness, every declared record surface readable (a declared-but-unreadable surface is a cannot-evaluate FINDING, never nothing-to-check), and merge-pending rows against first-parent merge evidence; with a registry present, also a registry the loader reports bad and the truncation guard's deny at its scope check for a Bash call from the repository root (the same finding list tools/orch_doctor.py --resume-audit writes): a root git resolves but the walk cannot carry out (for example one this process can enter but not read) arms the barrier in EVERY mode (where the session cwd is missing, empty or not a string, or git resolves no root for it, for any reason, such as an unreadable or broken config, a dangling gitfile, a dubious-ownership refusal, no git binary, a timeout, or a cwd this process cannot enter, or git exits 0 but prints output that cannot be decoded, is empty, or is not absolute, the audit returns silently in both modes before it reads the registry, and for a non-empty string cwd whether the truncation guard's scope check denies a Bash call from it depends only on its own ancestor walk of that cwd and the mode; git can still resolve a root this process cannot enter, through core.worktree from a session cwd inside the repository's git directory, and the audit then warns and arms the barrier in both modes where that root exists without search permission or is not a directory, because the registry loader reports it bad (as it does for a regular file named .aiqt at any root), and stays silent where that root does not exist, because the loader reports the registry absent), and an absent or unconfirmable registry scope (a symlinked registry, for example) arms it when AIQT_ORCH_REQUIRE_REGISTRY selects registry-required mode, so this layer is mode-sensitive. The barrier does not record that mode, so the two writers agree only when run with the same value; a doctor run without it can clear a barrier a registry-required SessionStart armed for a scope deny; clearing it does not allow any Bash call, because the barrier only warns and the guard denies on its own scope check. Arming and clearing are BEST-EFFORT and ATOMIC: both writers create a temporary file beside the barrier file, flush and fsync it, then rename it onto the barrier file with os.replace. Where the barrier cannot be written (its state directory cannot be created, the temporary file cannot be created or written, or the rename fails, for example XDG_STATE_HOME naming a regular file, or a full disk), the SessionStart audit removes the temporary file it created and ignores the error so SessionStart never wedges, the previous barrier file (armed or clear) or its absence is left byte-identical, the PreToolUse barrier therefore does not surface this run's findings, and the session still sees the SessionStart warning naming them (where opening the forced-exit log fails other than as not found, because the state directory cannot be searched or is not a directory, as with that regular file, the warning also names the forced-exit log as unreadable), and that warning then also says the barrier was not persisted (this audit did not arm it) and asks for a manual record instead of saying a re-run clears the barrier, naming the remedy (remove a directory at the barrier path, which neither audit can replace; otherwise make the state directory creatable and writable), while a clean audit that cannot clear the barrier adds no warning (a barrier it leaves armed still reads as armed, noted once per arming where its warned flag can be written, otherwise on each mutation outside the record surfaces, so one already warned about stays silent; a directory in its place reads as armed and is noted on each mutation outside the record surfaces); tools/orch_doctor.py --resume-audit does not ignore that error, its run ends with it, and the previous barrier file is left unchanged. The PreToolUse barrier reads the barrier file only where the registry loader reads the registry ok, and reads a barrier file that exists but is unreadable or malformed as armed (see orch-resume-barrier). Registry-scoped: silent where the registry loader reads the root's registry as absent; a root the loader cannot examine reads bad, not absent, and the audit warns. It reads records, git state, and the truncation guard's registry discovery only; it cannot detect a handoff that is stale in ways its declared grammar does not carry (free-text drift). Lease MISMATCH detection at this audit stays bounded to staleness, over the file mtime and, where the registry declares a lease heartbeat block, the declared heartbeat field too (an invalid declaration, an unevaluable heartbeat, and a stale or future heartbeat field are findings): these probes are shared with tools/orch_doctor.py --resume-audit, which runs with no session identity, so the holder field is not compared HERE; where the lease declares holder_is_session_id, each lease-scoped guard proves the payload session identity against the holder field per event, and the orch-lease-heartbeat controls surface a lost or taken lease to the session that last provably held it.

The mutation barrier behind orch-resume-audit, shipped WARN-FIRST (stage bake, a recorded posture): while the barrier state is armed it surfaces a systemMessage on the first mutation outside the allowlist (the record surfaces, the registry files, and the suite's own state directory stay writable, so the only exit, correcting the record, is never blocked), and it blocks nothing during the bake. The flip to deny is a manifest edit (stage to enforce, default to ask/deny) taken on recorded guard-events evidence after the bake period, per the guardrail-config-integrity discipline. Bash targets are not path-judged (a command's write targets are not lexically resolvable), so Bash mutations pass with the same surfacing only. Clearing the barrier requires re-running the audit (tools/orch_doctor.py --resume-audit) against corrected records; acknowledgement alone does not clear it. An absent barrier file (a dangling symlink included) reads as clear, and a symlink to a regular file reads as that file. The barrier is read with a non-blocking open (a FIFO with no writer does not wait for one), an fstat that refuses anything not a regular file before any read (so a FIFO or a device such as /dev/zero is never read), and a read bounded at 64 KiB. One that exists but is not a regular file (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory, or a symlink to any of these), is larger than the bound, cannot be read or parsed for any reason (including a RecursionError from deeply nested JSON), or is not a well-formed barrier (a JSON object whose keys are exactly a boolean active and a list of string findings, both required, plus an optional boolean warned and an optional string ts; a truncated write by an earlier writer is not), reads as ARMED, not absent: every mutation outside the allowlist then surfaces a note naming the file as unreadable or malformed with the reason (not once per arming, since there is no readable warned flag to record), which blocks nothing during the bake, and a mutation on the allowlist is allowed after the same read (a regular file on a filesystem that stalls, such as a hung network mount, can still stall the read until the hook timeout, as any file read can); it clears when the doctor's --resume-audit or the next SessionStart audit replaces the file (the rename replaces a FIFO, a device node or a symlink at the path and leaves a symlink's target intact), or when the user corrects or removes it (the state directory is on the allowlist), and where the state directory cannot be searched the replace fails too, so the note persists until its permissions are restored. Neither audit can replace a directory at the barrier path itself (the rename fails with IsADirectoryError), so for a directory the note says to remove the directory; a symlink to a directory gets the generic note, since the rename replaces the link. A writer removes the temporary file it created when any later step fails (writing, closing or renaming it) and never removes a temporary name it did not create; a process killed between creating and renaming it leaves that temporary file beside the barrier file. Recording the warned flag replaces the file atomically too; a failed replace leaves it unchanged, so the note surfaces again on the next mutation. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took under 0.01 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. A fired timer or an existing cron is never counted as a live task or a blocker. A RECORDING substrate, not an enforcement point: it appends launch rows (a Bash call with run_in_background true, or a registry-declared dispatch tool) and completion rows (a TaskOutput read) to the machine-written dispatch ledger the stop guard consumes as its Gap-B oracle. It never blocks; a failed ledger write is surfaced as a non-blocking systemMessage, never swallowed, and a lease max_age_hours horizon that cannot be evaluated does not turn this recorder off: the row is recorded anyway and the cannot-evaluate is surfaced as a note (armed and surfaced, never a silent skip). Coverage is exactly the hooked tools: a launch through an unhooked tool is invisible (costing one spurious stop-guard deny), a completion that never passes through TaskOutput is invisible until the staleness horizon expires the row, and the task-id extraction from tool responses is best-effort field matching. Both blind-spot directions are bounded by staleness plus the resume audit, and disclosed at the stop guard.

AIRTIGHT-NARROW (maintainer-directed simplification): this guard does NO shell parsing, so no lexical, quoting, or operator edge can make it credit a capture that does not exist. Within the registry scope (the REGISTRY-SCOPE RESIDUAL and REGISTRY-REQUIRED MODE below change only the outcome when no registry is found), it governs a background dispatch (run_in_background is true) with the capture-proof test below, and adds ONE narrow foreground branch (L-GS1): a foreground call (run_in_background not true) is out of scope EXCEPT that a bare '&' control operator, which detaches a child into asynchronous work this tool call does not track, is a DENY-and-educate steering the operator to the tracked background dispatch (run_in_background) or to running it in the foreground and waiting. That foreground detector is a dedicated quote- and escape-tracking scan (not the shared segmenter, which strips quote and escape provenance and would misread a quoted or escaped ampersand as a separator): it distinguishes the detach '&' from the shell forms that also carry an ampersand but do not detach ('&&', '&>', '&>>', '<&', '>&', '|&', and any single-quoted, double-quoted, or backslash-escaped ampersand, and an '&' inside an unquoted word-start '#' comment, which is dropped). Where a '#' opens a comment is read under two rules, the historical one (after any Unicode whitespace character) and bash's (only after a space, tab, newline, or shell metacharacter), and a detach seen under either rule DENIES, so the bash rule only adds denies: a '#' after a carriage return, vertical tab, form feed, no-break space, 0x1c-0x1f separator, NEL, or other Unicode space is not a comment to bash and the '&' after it is caught. It looks ONLY for a bare '&' operator at the outer quoting level AS ITS OWN QUOTE TRACKING READS IT; where that reading diverges from bash's, a bare outer '&' is missed (the false-allow residual below, whose list of known cases is not complete). A scan that ENDS still inside an unbalanced quote (including one left open by an ANSI-C dollar-single-quote construct ($'...') this scan does not model, or by an apostrophe in a here-document body) could hide a real trailing '&', so it FAILS TOWARD THE DENY, with a reason naming the open quote rather than a bare '&'; this covers only a quote still open at the end, not one misread in mid-string. KNOWN FALSE-ALLOW RESIDUAL (confirmed against real bash; the scanner docstring lists the same cases): the scan reads only the outer quoting level, and its quote and comment tracking can diverge from bash's in further ways than those listed here, so this list is NOT complete. Known cases include a real detach that is NOT seen and is SILENTLY ALLOWED (1) when its '&' sits inside a command substitution or backtick wrapped in double quotes (echo "$(job &)"); (2) inside a string that eval or quote removal re-reads as code (e'v'al 'job &', {eval,} 'job &', \eval 'job &'); (3) after an ANSI-C $'...' quote with an escaped quote that leaves the scan balanced but misaligned; (4) inside an arithmetic subscript that runs a substitution; (5) QUOTE SHIFT: after a quote character that bash reads as data but the scan reads as a quote, above all an apostrophe or double quote in a here-document body (quoted delimiter or not, including the double-quoted commit-message form), which flips the scan's quote state so that a LATER real bare '&' (between two here-documents, or before a second stray quote that rebalances the scan) reads as quoted text and is allowed; and (6) COMMENT SHIFT: after a '#' that follows a blank inside an unquoted ${...} parameter expansion, which bash reads as expansion text but the scan reads as a comment start, so a real bare '&' later on that line is skipped (echo ${x:- #} & job, echo ${line%% #*} & job). HONEST RESIDUAL (disclose-guard-residuals): detachment achieved WITHOUT a bare '&' in the outer command is NOT caught and is SILENTLY ALLOWED, not over-denied - a runtime detacher that backgrounds with no '&' (setsid, disown, coproc; nohup is normally written with a trailing '&', which IS caught), a nested shell string whose '&' sits inside quotes (bash -c '... &'), and an alias or function that renames a detacher; the grammar cases that OVER-fire instead are NOT a single case: any unquoted '&' this scan does not model as a detach still reaches the scan and reads as an operator, so it DENIES when no detach is present. Examples are a here-document body carrying a literal '&', and an arithmetic expansion such as $(( a & b )) where '&' is bitwise-AND; any other construct this scan does not model that leaves a non-detach '&' unquoted in the outer string over-DENIES the same way. OVER-REFUSAL OF SAFE HERE-DOCUMENTS (disclosed): the scan reads a here-document body as code even under a quoted delimiter (<<'EOF'), so a safe here-document whose body carries an unquoted '&' (Fix A & B) or an unbalanced apostrophe (the user's file) is DENIED although nothing detaches; in the git commit-message form wrapped in double quotes the body is read as double-quoted text and each double quote in the body toggles that reading, so whether a body '&' is denied depends on where it falls relative to those quotes (say "a & b" is denied, say "hi" & bye is allowed). The remedy is to write the text to a file and pass the file. This misreading is NOT only in the safe direction: the same body quotes cause the quote-shift false-allow (5) above. The guard locates its registry scope by the UNION of two legs: a walk of the session cwd's physical ancestor chain with no-follow, descriptor-anchored lookups, and, where git DOES resolve a toplevel for the cwd (the scrubbed rev-parse primitive the sibling orchestration guards root via), that toplevel's registry too, because core.worktree (set in a repository config or a gitfile's gitdir target) can point the work tree OFF the cwd's ancestor chain, where the walk alone never visits its registry (a review finding: from inside such a repository's metadata directory the walk alone turned the old rev-parse scoping's deny into an allow); BY DEFAULT git success can only ADD a deny, a git failure alone never denies, and the walk alone still decides where git cannot run or answer, while in the opt-in registry-required mode below a git failure where the registry is reachable only through the git toplevel reads as ABSENT and is denied, and git success can then remove that deny; the AIRTIGHT-NARROW claim is about the command-string analysis doing NO shell parsing. Overriding that DENY does not itself create tracking; only converting to run_in_background=true lets the dispatch ledger record the launch. The foreground branch stays registry-scoped, so BY DEFAULT a non-orchestrated session acquires no bare-'&' deny and no prompt and only the pre-scope denies below (a malformed or control-character tool_name, a malformed cwd, or a registry walk that cannot be carried out) apply in every session; in the opt-in registry-required mode below a session with no registry found is instead denied on every Bash call that passes those checks. REGISTRY-SCOPE RESIDUAL (disclose-guard-residuals, decided against check-fails-closed-on-unreadable): the orchestration registry is the whole suite's scope declaration, not an input this guard is declared to cover, and the hook is wired by installing the pack in every session, orchestrated or not; so with NO registry entry on the cwd's physical ancestor chain (.aiqt/orchestration.local.json and .aiqt/orchestration.json a clean not-found at every chain directory, judged by a no-follow, descriptor-anchored walk of that chain and its path-anchored recheck) AND none at a git-resolved toplevel (the union leg above) the guard is, BY DEFAULT, INERT and silently ALLOWS every Bash call that passes the pre-scope checks below (a readable tool_name and a walkable cwd; in the opt-in registry-required mode below it DENIES them instead), including a real bare-'&' detach, a truncating-sink background dispatch, and a malformed tool_input, and including a session whose GIT DISCOVERY FAILS (no git binary on PATH, a dubious-ownership refusal, a broken global config, a bare repository, a cwd inside a .git directory, a discovery timeout or error): BY DEFAULT a git failure alone is out of this guard's scope, never a deny (the earlier lockout, where any such failure denied every Bash call and the denied session could not even run the git or install command that repairs it, is withdrawn); in registry-required mode a git failure where the registry is reachable only through the git toplevel reads as ABSENT and is denied. Failing closed there BY DEFAULT would deny Bash in every non-orchestrated repository. REGISTRY-REQUIRED MODE (opt-in; default unchanged): an adopter who wants exactly that fail-closed posture sets the environment variable AIQT_ORCH_REQUIRE_REGISTRY (any value except an explicit off: '', '0', 'false', 'no', 'off', ASCII case-insensitive and matched exactly with nothing stripped, so an off word padded with a space, tab, newline, or no-break space reads as ON; a garbled value reads as ON, the deny-safe direction for an explicitly configured strict mode), and an ABSENT registry (no chain entry and no git-toplevel entry) then fails closed on every Bash call that passes the pre-scope checks, denying it with a reason naming the mode and its repair (commit the registry, run from inside the orchestrated tree, or unset the variable); a registry discovery that cannot be evaluated (the three-valued discovery below) is denied the same way, with a reason naming the unconfirmable entry and its repair. It is an environment variable rather than a pack config key because every pack config surface is a per-repo file located by the same cwd-anchored lookup whose empty result this mode exists to fail closed on, so a file-based key cannot speak exactly when it is needed; the hook's execution environment is the one channel independent of that lookup. A tree that wants this control commits the registry; the walk finds it from any cwd under the tree, with or without a working git, so the same dubious-ownership, missing-git, or broken-config session INSIDE an orchestrated tree still applies the guard. The walk does not stop at the repository root or a filesystem boundary (git discovery stops at a mount point), so a registry in ANY ancestor directory - above a nested repository, above a mount point, or in a non-git tree - scopes the guard in; it is the UNION with the git-toplevel leg, not the walk alone, that makes this scoping a deny-safe widening over the old rev-parse scoping (the walk alone removed the old scoping's deny where core.worktree points the work tree off the cwd's ancestor chain; with the union, git success can only add coverage, and BY DEFAULT a git failure alone never removes a deny; in registry-required mode added coverage can remove the absent-registry deny, and a git failure that hides a registry reachable only through the git toplevel adds one). CONCURRENT-MOVE DETECTION AND ITS BOUND: descriptor anchoring preserves each opened directory's identity, not its parent relationship, so a mid-walk rename of an ancestor could redirect the walk past a continuously present registry; a walk that finds nothing therefore re-resolves the chain BY PATH and re-probes every chain directory, scoping the session IN when that recheck finds a registry and DENYING (never allowing) when the re-resolved dev/ino chain does not match the chain the walk visited or cannot be re-resolved. The race limit is disclosed, not closed: the walk, the recheck, and the Bash call they gate are not one atomic step, and neither the walk nor the recheck is one atomic read of the chain (each is a sequence of lookups), so two windows are out of view. (1) DURING the walk and the recheck: a concurrent rename of an ancestor directory timed against the walk AND the recheck can hide a registry and the call is then allowed (denied under registry-required mode), for example a registry relocated within the chain so it is never where either pass probes, or a sibling directory swapped in under a textual chain path during the recheck so that it reports the same dev/ino the redirected walk recorded and the two chains agree. (2) AFTER the recheck returns: any change to the chain or a registry - including a registry that appears only then - is out of view, as it is for any pre-execution check. Both windows are outside this guard's threat model: it exists to stop ACCIDENTAL truncation in an orchestrated tree, and a party able to rename this host's ancestor directories concurrently with the hook is not that case; a mid-walk rename that is not also timed against the recheck is caught (a found or a deny), and no further race machinery is added. A directory bind-mounted onto its own child repeats one dev/ino between parent and child without being the filesystem root; the walk steps THROUGH such a repeat rather than misreading it as the root (only the filesystem root's own identity ends the walk, and a walk the root identity cannot bound fails closed at its depth bound), so a registry above the mount point is still reached - verified by simulation, since these hosts cannot create mounts, with the path-anchored recheck as the behavioural backstop (an fd-walk miss at a mount edge surfaces as a found or a deny on the recheck, never an allow). Registry discovery is THREE-VALUED: a chain or toplevel entry is cleanly ABSENT, a CONFIRMED registry (the first registry name present in a real '.aiqt' directory, the local name first, is a regular file under a no-follow stat, whatever its content), or CANNOT-EVALUATE (a '.aiqt' chain entry that is a symlink, a regular file, or a directory this process lacks search (execute) permission on, such as mode 0600 or 0000 for a process those modes bind (mode 0100 evaluates normally for its owner where O_PATH exists and for a process the mode bits do not bind, such as root or one holding CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH or CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE; it cannot be evaluated by any other process that is not its owner, nor by its owner where the O_RDONLY fallback, which also needs read permission, is in use), a first present registry name that is not a regular file or whose no-follow stat faults, or a git-resolved toplevel that exists but cannot be opened; one that does not exist reads as absent). BY DEFAULT a cannot-evaluate entry reads as PRESENT and keeps the guard ACTIVE, never inert, exactly as a PRESENT registry that cannot be read or validated (a read or parse error, or a non-version-1 object) keeps it ACTIVE; in the opt-in registry-required mode a cannot-evaluate entry is NOT a registry, so a Bash call that passes the pre-scope checks is DENIED there (the walk stops at the nearest non-absent chain entry, so a cannot-evaluate entry there denies in that mode even where a registry sits further up the chain or at the git toplevel; with nothing on the chain, a cannot-evaluate git toplevel denies), so a discovery fault never satisfies that mode, while a confirmed registry satisfies it whether or not it can be read or validated. MALFORMED OR UNWALKABLE INPUT FAILS CLOSED (check-fails-closed-on-unreadable): a tool_name that is missing, null, empty, not a string, or carrying a NUL or any other control character (a control character never appears in a real tool name, so such a name is never read as an ordinary non-Bash tool); a cwd that is missing, null, empty, or not a string; and a string cwd whose registry walk cannot be carried out (it contains a NUL, is not an existing directory this process can read and enter, or has an ancestor directory the walk cannot open or examine) are DENIED with a reason naming the defect and an action that repairs it, before the registry scope is read, so in every session, orchestrated or not, while a plain non-Bash string tool_name is out of scope; within scope, a tool_input that is missing, null, or not a JSON object, a run_in_background that is present but not a real boolean (the string "true" is malformed, never read as foreground), and a foreground command that is not a string are each DENIED with a reason naming the defect; an omitted run_in_background is a foreground call. A background dispatch is ALLOWED only when the whole command is drawn from a conservative safe character set (letters, digits, space and tab, and the punctuation '_ - . / = : @ , + %'), so it carries NO shell metacharacter (no pipe, redirect, separator, quote, expansion, command or process substitution, grouping, glob, comment, tilde, history, or newline) and is not a shell reserved word (coproc, which backgrounds a coprocess whose output the harness does not capture, or a compound/prefix keyword such as if/for/while/time) and its full stdout reaches the harness capture that run_in_background binds to the TaskOutput completion signal IN THE COMMON CASE - unless the invoked program or wrapper itself detaches, daemonizes, or redirects that output, which is out of view (see the program-behaviour residual below). ANY other command is ALLOWED WITH AN INFORMATIONAL NOTE: the guard does not parse shell syntax to prove or disprove capture, and an unprovable background dispatch is not a hazard (a dispatch that redirects or pipes its own output is a normal, legitimate form), so it allows and notes that the operator should make sure the full output lands in a durable capture (redirect the producer's own stdout to a real file, or make a real-file tee the final stage). DISCLOSED COVERAGE BOUND (deliberate, not a defect): this trades COVERAGE for an assurance of NO SHELL-SYNTAX FALSE-ALLOW (no quoting or parsing edge in the dispatch string can fabricate a capture). A legitimate captured background dispatch that uses any shell syntax (a real-file redirect, a tee, a glob, an env-assignment prefix carrying a quote) is ALLOWED WITH A NOTE rather than proven; the guard DENIES a background dispatch on capture grounds ONLY when it pipes a producer into a TRUNCATING SINK (head/tail), which discards the producer's full output and exit status (a review finding); the sink is resolved THROUGH leading shell command-modifier wrappers (command/env/builtin/exec/nice/nohup/stdbuf/time and their own option/assignment args) so a sink hidden behind one (| command head, | env head) is still caught (a review finding), while a wrapper resolving to a non-truncating command still allows-with-note; and otherwise the informational note and the vrfdlv delivery-marker discipline are the compensating layers. What this buys over a lexical capture-proof: the ALLOW rests on a raw-character test that no quoting or parsing can fool, so there is no shell-syntax edge that can silently open a false allow. The residual is RUNTIME behaviour beyond the dispatch string: a plain command can still fail to deliver its full output to durable capture for reasons no pre-execution command-string check can show. Two classes. (a) The invoked program or wrapper's own behaviour - a terminal multiplexer or setsid that detaches, a start-stop-daemon or nohup-style wrapper that backgrounds or redirects the producer's stdout (e.g. --output /dev/null), a program that internally pipes to head/tail, or one that sources a script or resolves a PATH name to a truncating tool. (b) Platform and resource limits - the harness's own TaskOutput capture has a size ceiling (Claude Code terminates a background task whose output exceeds a documented limit), so a very large stream is lost at the harness regardless of the command, and disk-full, a kill signal, or other run-time conditions can likewise cut delivery short. None of this appears in the command string. The guard's ALLOW therefore asserts only that no shell SYNTAX in the dispatch string can defeat capture; whether the output actually and fully reaches durable capture is a run-time property that the post-execution vrfdlv delivery-marker discipline, not this guard, confirms. The guard DENIES exactly these. In every session (pre-scope): a tool_name that is missing, null, empty, not a string, or carrying a NUL or another control character; and a cwd that is missing, null, empty, or not a string, contains a NUL, is not an existing directory this process can read and enter, has an ancestor directory the registry walk cannot open or examine, or has an ancestor chain that changed while the walk read it. Only within the registry scope: a tool_input that is not a JSON object; a run_in_background that is present but not a boolean; a foreground command that is not a string; a FOREGROUND command whose scan ends inside an open quote, denied with a reason naming the open quote; a FOREGROUND bare-'&' detach (untracked asynchronous work, steered to a tracked run_in_background dispatch or to a foreground wait), which with the open-quote deny also covers the over-refusals above; a BACKGROUND dispatch whose command is not a string or is empty; and a BACKGROUND dispatch that pipes a producer into a TRUNCATING SINK (head/tail), whose completion signal would bind to the sink's truncated output so a failing producer would read as a clean, finished run (a review finding). Each malformed-input deny carries a reason naming the defect. Under opt-in registry-required mode only (AIQT_ORCH_REQUIRE_REGISTRY set): every Bash call that passes the pre-scope checks when no orchestration registry is found (including a registry reachable only through the git toplevel when git fails, which reads as not found), and every such call whose registry discovery cannot be evaluated (a '.aiqt' that is a regular file, a symlink, or a directory without search (execute) permission, a first present registry name that is not a regular file or cannot be stat'ed, or a git toplevel that exists but cannot be opened), denied with a reason naming the mode and its repair. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 1.19 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

Registry-scoped deny companion to orch-truncation-guard's bare-& DENY-and-educate (defence in depth on the same PreToolUse Bash event): inert with no orchestration registry at the session cwd's git-resolved toplevel (it roots there only, with no ancestor walk and no union, so it is inert where git resolves no toplevel, or where the truncation guard's walk finds a registry above or beside the toplevel; it never reads AIQT_ORCH_REQUIRE_REGISTRY, so it stays inert on an absent registry in that mode too), and NOT lease-scoped (a bounded worker building a fire-and-forget poll is equally wrong). It DENIES only an UNAMBIGUOUS canonical shape recognized by a best-effort LEXICAL heuristic, a status-polling loop detached with a SINGLE bare '&' that is the command's FINAL operator: exactly ONE for/while/until loop closed by a bare-'&' 'done', whose body carries a 'sleep' command word and whose construct (the loop condition through 'done') carries a status probe. The probe test is a deliberate HEURISTIC, not an enumeration of every status tool: a 'gh' or 'curl' command word, a '--watch' token, or a token with an 'actions/runs' path component; a poll driven by another probe command is a disclosed miss, not a match. Reserved words (for/while/until/do/done) are recognized ONLY as the EXACT raw-unquoted token: because argv is quote-decoded and the command-word helper basenames, a bare '&' closing a command whose name was written quoted, or a path such as '/tmp/done', is NOT read as the loop terminator (it classifies 'none'), and an inner loop header that shares a segment with the outer 'do' is still counted from the raw-unquoted tokens rather than borrowing the outer loop's probe. The classifier is THREE-VALUED over the shared quote/redirect-aware lexer (_lex_command). It is 'none' on a full parse that is simply not the canonical shape: no bare '&'; a bare '&' that does not close a raw-unquoted 'done' terminator (for example 'sleep 30 &', a quoted or path 'done', or a 'done' carrying a redirect such as 'done >log &'); or a clean single loop lacking the sleep or the probe. It is 'indeterminate', emitting nothing and deferring to the truncation guard's generic bare-'&' DENY-and-educate on the same event, whenever the structure cannot be soundly attributed to one canonical loop, so it never fabricates a deny: an unparseable construct (heredoc, here-string, process substitution, unbalanced quote, NUL, malformed redirect); any subshell or C-style '(( ))' grouping (a '(' or ')' separator); more than one bare '&'; a command trailing the bare-'&' 'done'; a nested or extra loop keyword (a second for/while/until/do or a second 'done', counted from the raw-unquoted tokens); a conditional reserved word (if/then/elif/else/fi/case/esac or a '!' negation) anywhere in the loop span; or brace grouping ('{' or '}') in the loop span. This conservative posture is deliberate for a BLOCK guard: a false 'match' would strand a session, so any ambiguity defers to the truncation guard rather than denying here. HONEST RESIDUALS (disclose-guard-residuals): detachment with no bare '&' in the outer command (setsid, disown, coproc, an aliased or function-renamed detacher, a nested bash -c '... &'), and a poll loop hidden inside a command substitution (opaque to the segment walk), are NOT caught and are silently allowed here; a nested loop, a conditional or brace-grouped body, a C-style for '(( ))', a multi-detach command, and a subshell-grouped or unparseable detach are 'indeterminate' here and left to the truncation guard's DENY-and-educate, not denied by this hook. Quoting is derived from raw character positions (argv_opaque flags an unquoted expansion/glob/brace/tilde but NOT plain quoting), so the raw-unquoted reserved-word checks read seg.raw directly. Fail-open (silent allow) on a non-Bash or absent tool, no git toplevel, an absent registry, and a non-string or empty command; a present-but-malformed registry leaves the guard active (deny-safe direction). The 'trkasy' rule text already carries the untracked-wait-loop clause; this hook enforces it and adds no rule. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took about 1.00 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

A RECORDING substrate: stamps the clock-read UTC time of each GENUINE human prompt into turn-state (resetting the stop guard's deny counters), classifies a prompt matching a registered wake as timer-originated (not stamping it), and injects a measured-gap context line so any quiet-duration reasoning uses the measured figure. It never blocks, and a lease max_age_hours horizon that cannot be evaluated does not turn this recorder off: the stamp or classification proceeds anyway and the cannot-evaluate is surfaced as a note (armed and surfaced, never a silent skip). Turn-state is saved through the state directory opened once as a directory descriptor (with O_PATH where the platform has it, an open that needs no permission on that directory itself, only search permission on its ancestors, while the later stat, create, rename and cleanup need search permission on it, the last three write permission too; where O_PATH is absent the fallback open also needs read permission on that directory), every later step bound to it, so that directory swapped for a symlink after the open cannot redirect the save or its cleanup (the directory path itself is resolved once, at that open, a directory moved after the open still receives the save under its new name, and the writing uid is not a boundary): the hook creates a temporary file of its own beside turn-state.json (an exclusive create under a random name that never follows a symlink, so nothing already at a temporary-like name is written or removed), giving it the existing file's permission bits (0600 for a new file), writing and fsyncing it, and renaming it onto turn-state.json: a reader sees the previous file or the new one, never a part of either, and a failed save leaves the previous file (or its absence) in place and is named with its error in the note, which also names a temporary file whose removal after the failure failed, by the state directory path as given, which after a swap may no longer lead to it (one left by a process killed mid-save is removed by nothing). Concurrent saves never share a temporary file, but the last rename wins, so two hooks that update turn-state at once can lose one update (the read-modify-write is not serialized) while each reports its save as succeeded. Where turn-state cannot be written, a genuine prompt still proceeds, with a note saying its time was not stamped and the deny counters were not reset, and a timer-originated prompt's context line and a systemMessage say consuming its wake digest failed, so a later prompt with the same text may read as timer-originated or as genuine human input. Classification is digest matching against wake registrations this suite itself recorded: a wake fired through a mechanism the suite never saw is stamped as genuine human input (the safe direction: it only narrows guard autonomy). An unknown prior stamp yields an 'unknown' gap that authorizes nothing.

The scheduled-yield binding of the decision core: a call that parks the run (schedule_idle) or ends the loop (a ScheduleWakeup with stop=true is classified stop) is judged against a fresh enumeration. Registry-scoped and lease-scoped like orch-stop-guard; a tool the registry's yield_tools list does not name is out of scope even inside the matcher, and a registry yield tool OUTSIDE this fixed matcher is NOT covered (the doctor flags it; a manifest matcher is fixed at generation). On the schedule path a cannot-evaluate DENIES (missing evidence never licenses new autonomy; a denied tool call cannot wedge a session), bounded by a three-denial cap on an unchanged basis, after which it ALLOWS WITH FINDINGS so the guard cannot be farmed into bypass training. Each deny, the quiet-claim deny included, appends a guard-events row; a failed append leaves no row and adds a short recording-failure warning to the deny reason and the banner while the deny stands. The cap, and the loop bound of a stop=true call, are judged on the count the call reads from turn-state.json before any save, and only a saved denial adds to it. A save needs a state directory the hook can write and search, and read where the platform lacks O_PATH. Every owner-mode list in this residue holds for a hook that runs without root as the state directory's owner and holds neither CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, which searches and writes the directory in every mode, nor CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, which searches it and reads turn-state.json in every mode, with the state directory on a filesystem mounted read-write and not marked immutable, since a read-only mount or an immutable directory fails every save: of the eight owner modes of the state directory, 0300 and 0700 save with O_PATH and only 0700 saves without it. A deny whose denial counter cannot be written leaves the count on disk unchanged and says so in its deny reason and banner (it does not count toward the cap, or toward the loop bound for a stop=true call); the deny stands. A state directory the hook cannot search (0000, 0200, 0400 and 0600) reads as a fresh turn-state, with no count and no recorded basis, so a count already earned there is not seen; a turn-state.json that cannot be read or does not hold a JSON object, in a state directory the hook can search, reads as a schedule count of zero with no recorded basis, and as the loop bound reached for a stop=true call, and a deny saved over it starts the count afresh at one. So a schedule call the decision core would deny allows with findings exactly when the count it reads is at or above the cap on an unchanged basis (a schedule_denials value that validation rejects reads as zero, and a stop_hook_active field has no effect on a schedule call), and a stop=true call does so exactly when one of four holds: the count it reads is at or above the loop bound; turn-state.json cannot be read, or does not hold a JSON object, in a state directory the hook can search; its stop_denials value is present but is not a JSON integer from 0 to 9999 (for example a float such as 1.0, a boolean, a string, null, a negative number or a number above 9999), which reads as the loop bound; or the call's payload carries a stop_hook_active field set to the JSON value true, which relieves it whatever the mode of the state directory (the Claude Code hooks reference documents that field in the Stop input and does not list it in the PreToolUse input, so a stop=true call is relieved this way only by a payload that carries it anyway). Relief already earned therefore survives a later save failure only while the state directory stays searchable and turn-state.json readable (0100 and 0500, and 0300 without O_PATH, relieve a schedule call and name its failed wake-digest save in the note), and is lost while the state directory cannot be searched (0000, 0200, 0400 and 0600 deny, the count on disk unchanged). No relief reaches the quiet-duration deny or the unreadable-registry deny: both are decided before the decision core, so both deny a schedule call even with a readable count at or above the cap on an unchanged basis, and the unreadable-registry deny also denies a stop=true call that any of the four loop-bound triggers would relieve, a stop_hook_active field set to true included (the quiet-duration deny judges only schedule calls); the quiet-duration deny needs the measured gap in turn-state.json, so a state directory the hook cannot search never reaches it. An allowed schedule whose wake digest cannot be written to turn-state says so in its note (the returning prompt may then read as genuine human input or as timer-originated, so the note promises neither); neither failure changes the decision. Wake hygiene: a permitted schedule must name the tracked item or blocker it will recheck in its own text, judged by token containment (a paraphrase that names neither id nor ref denies once, a disclosed over-fire). The quiet-duration check is a best-effort regex: it fires only when the call text carries a parseable minutes claim AND turn-state carries a measured gap, and then the measured figure wins; an unparseable claim or an unknown measured endpoint authorizes nothing and is not invented. A fired timer or an existing cron is never counted as a live task or a blocker. Escape-sentinel acceptance, the attestation narrowing of external and foreign-lease evidence, and the anti-shrinkage checkpoint are shared with orch-stop-guard; cap or bound relief past any non-closed disposition (actionable, cannot-evaluate, waiting, blocked, or proposed) is marked forced_unresolved (a guard-events row plus an append-only row in forced-exit.jsonl, normally raised once, at least once if recording it in forced-exit-surfaced.json fails), a failed record surfacing in the returned systemMessage. DEADLINE: main() gives this check 8 seconds (the 10-second hook timeout less 2), counted from before its payload read, and fails closed with exit 2 when it has not decided by then; on the worst shapes the hooks self-test times, up to 1 MB, its slowest call took under 0.01 s in-process on a 24-core host with Python 3.14.4 (2026-10-15). Interpreter start-up and a wait the interpreter cannot interrupt (a read from a hung mount, a long call into C code) fall outside that deadline, and whether the platform blocks a call whose hook it stops at its own timeout is unverified. Where SIGALRM, setitimer or the main thread is unavailable, or SIGALRM is blocked, the check runs with no deadline; cleanup that runs while the deadline unwinds is outside it.

Registry scoped and inert without a review dispatch binding. It checks only a provably plain dispatch, decided on the raw characters by the shared plain-command specification: printable ASCII only, no shell character outside a single-quoted segment, a double-quoted segment holding none, words separated by spaces, and a bare, unquoted command word that is a declared dispatch command (compared without regard to case), so the dispatch is the only command of the call (no operator, no redirection, not even </dev/null), with the brief given once and last (a short brief option never in its = form). In a session a binding scopes, every Bash call that is not one plain command is withheld as UNVERIFIABLE, whatever it names, since a dispatcher name assembled at run time is not in the raw text, and so is a plain command that names a declared command other than as its command word; this refuses many harmless commands (a pipeline, a redirection, a variable, a glob, a mention such as grep of the command name). A plain command's word is a bare name, or a path whose directory is /usr/bin, /bin, /usr/local/bin or /usr/sbin, of a declared dispatch command or a program on an allowlist (git, opf, and programs that cannot run another, such as ls, cat, grep, cp, mv and rm); every other program (a shell, an interpreter at any version, find, sed, tar, sort, make, cd, an undeclared dispatcher) is withheld as well. A plain command whose program runs an argument or its configuration as shell text (a git alias set before the session, a package script) can still assemble a name the hook does not see. A brief path under /proc or /dev is withheld, since it can name a different file in the hook's process. A dispatch through an undeclared command, an alias, a function, a script that dispatches internally, a nested shell string, or a non-Bash tool is not seen and is allowed. A linked worktree is scoped by its main worktree's registry, located through git or, where git cannot run, through the raw .git and commondir files; a linked worktree whose main worktree cannot be located (a separated git directory, with git running or not) withholds every Bash call. A linked worktree of a bare repository (core.bare true) has no main worktree and is not withheld, and a failed git probe where the .git is a directory is no linked worktree, so a session with no registry anywhere is not withheld; a core.bare of true set in a separated git directory's configuration would end that withholding. A registry without a binding never ends the search: the session's registry, its main worktree's and every ancestor registry are read, nearest first, and the first binding on each way decides; each registry file is read on its own, so a local registry without a binding cannot hide the committed one's. In a bound session a plain command that names a registry file or the .aiqt directory is refused unless its command word only reads (cat, head, tail, wc, ls, stat, grep, cmp, diff); the directory counts as named through a value glued to a short option, a git pathspec after its magic, a quoted glob matching it (so a quoted * is refused too), a .. resolved against the cwd, or a subdirectory of it entered in a command whose words also climb with a .. component. A plain git command carrying an option or subcommand that runs a program, named in it or configured, is refused whatever it names, since that program's shell text can hold a name no word check sees: a global -p or --paginate, --ext-diff, --textconv, cat-file --filters, --show-signature, a %G placeholder (also with a modifier: %+G?, %-GG, % GK) or a %(signature) or %(*signature) atom in a --format or --pretty value or in a shortlog --group value (git reads a group holding % as a pretty format), a signature sort key (signature, -signature, v:*signature:grade, and any key holding the word, such as contents:signature, which is refused too) in a for-each-ref, branch or tag --sort value, grep -O or --open-files-in-pager, rebase -x or --exec, difftool -x or --extcmd, --upload-pack, --receive-pack, --exec (as archive and push take it), clone -u, -c or --config, send-email's --sendmail-cmd, --to-cmd, --cc-cmd, --header-cmd and --smtp-server, a global --exec-path=DIR, bisect run, submodule foreach and filter-branch, each long option abbreviated or not. A plain git command whose subcommand only reads (status, log, diff, show, rev-parse, ls-files, blame, grep, cat-file, or config in a read form), with no -c or --config-env global and no --output option, treats every word as data, so a registry name, a glob or a repository key in it is not refused, unless, for log, show and diff, an option asks for patch output (such as -p, -u, -U, -c, --patch or --cc), to which a textconv filter applies, which gets the full checks; options are read with their operands up to a -- ending them, so -Sconfig, --grep -c and -n 3 ask for none. A plain git command runs only a subcommand on a closed allowlist, matched exactly (status, log, diff, show, rev-parse, ls-files, ls-tree, cat-file, blame, grep, describe, shortlog, merge-base, rev-list, for-each-ref, show-ref, branch, tag, remote, config, add, rm, mv, commit, push, fetch, stash, switch, checkout, restore, reset, merge, rebase, cherry-pick, revert, worktree, clone), or is git alone or with only --version, --exec-path, --html-path, --man-path or --info-path; every other subcommand (instaweb, difftool, mergetool, send-email, filter-branch, bisect, submodule, daemon, web--browse, the credential commands, help, an alias, an external git-NAME program, one behind a global option the hook does not know) is refused, whatever it names.
